docs.title: Hangar
docs.text:
A self-hosted home for your arsenal of models.

Get started Try the demo

Hangar is a self-hosted model and dataset hub, compatible with the Hugging Face Hub API, git, Ollama and LM Studio. It keeps your machine learning models and datasets on your own storage, with full version history, and serves them to the tools you already use:

  • Hugging Face clients. Set HF_ENDPOINT, and huggingface_hub, the hf CLI, transformers, diffusers, sentence-transformers, datasets and vLLM work unchanged.
  • git. git clone and git push, with git-lfs.
  • Ollama. ollama pull hangar.example.com/org/model:Q4_K_M for any GGUF Repo.
  • LM Studio. hangar lmstudio install org/model:Q4_K_M.
  • Datasets. load_dataset, pandas and Polars over hf://, DuckDB over HTTPS, and a Dataset Viewer in the browser.

Teams use it as a private Ollama registry, as one model cache for everyone, to avoid Hugging Face rate limits in CI and to load models in Kubernetes without downloading them on every Pod start. Hugging Face does not sell an on-premises Hub; Hugging Face Hub on-premises explains how Hangar fills that gap.

Pull models and datasets from huggingface.co once, including only the quantisation, Config or Split you want and any code they depend on, then load them from fast local storage as often as you like. Each Pull keeps a Mirror with the upstream Repo ID and Commit SHAs, so code pinned to a Revision keeps working. Upload models that exist nowhere else. Browse everything you have, and everything you could pull, in one place.

To try the web UI without installing anything, open the demo. It runs on sample data, and nothing you do there is saved.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
docker run -d --name hangar -p 8080:8080 -v hangar:/var/lib/hangar \
  -e HANGAR_SERVER_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:8080 \
  ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:latest
docker cp hangar:/var/lib/hangar/secrets.yaml - | tar -xO | grep bootstrap_admin_password

Open http://localhost:8080, sign in as hangar-admin, and pull hf-internal-testing/tiny-random-bert from Discover. Then point your Python tools at Hangar, with transformers and torch installed:

export HF_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:8080
export HF_TOKEN=hgr_...   # create one under Settings, Tokens
python -c "from transformers import AutoModel; AutoModel.from_pretrained('hf-internal-testing/tiny-random-bert')"

Next: Get started covers Docker, Compose, Helm and the binary, your first sign-in and your first Pull.

docs.title: What it runs on
docs.text: Hangar runs as one container on a laptop or homelab, with SQLite and a local folder. It scales out to stateless replicas over Postgres and S3-compatible storage, with separate web and worker processes. It exports traces, metrics and logs with OpenTelemetry, and supports local accounts and OIDC sign-in. See Scaling.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text: Hangar stores and serves files; it does not run models. Spaces, the Inference API, Hugging Face Jobs, Buckets and kernels, SSH git and Xet downloads are out of scope. It accepts Xet uploads, so huggingface_hub with hf_xet installed works with no setup, but it stores whole files and serves them over plain HTTP.

docs.title: Licence
docs.text: Hangar is source-available under the Elastic License 2.0. You can use, change and self-host it, including inside your company. You can't offer it to others as a hosted or managed service, or remove licence notices.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
These are the load test results for Hangar's scale targets: the targets in the specification's architecture chapter and the scenarios in loadtest/, run as loadtest/README.md describes. They were measured on 17 October 2026 on a pre-release build of Hangar 1.0.0: the performance changes that were then merged into 1.0.0 as commit 40ad448. The Repo listings results, for 100,000 Repos per Instance, were measured on 21 and 22 October 2026 with an in-process load test. Releases since then have not been measured again.

The numbers come from one shared laptop, not dedicated hardware, so read them as evidence that a target holds or fails on modest hardware rather than as capacity figures. Deviations lists every way the setup differs from the reference setup.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Target Result Pass or fail HEAD /resolve p99 under 50 ms at 200 requests per second per replica p99 7 to 28 ms with the host lightly loaded; 87 to 206 ms when other workloads saturated the host Pass, with the host lightly loaded Model info p99 under 100 ms p99 12.5 to 62.7 ms Pass Full listing of a 100,000-file Repo under 10 seconds at p95 p95 6.15 to 6.79 s Pass Clone of a 10,000-Commit Repo under 30 seconds at p95 p95 0.60 to 1.13 s in the four runs with a kept p95 (five runs) Pass, see Clone errors Web replica memory flat and under 256 MiB during uploads peak 66 and 81 MiB during four concurrent 1 GiB uploads Pass (4 GiB uploaded, not 50 GiB) Web replica memory flat and under 256 MiB during downloads peak 104 and 115 MiB while downloading 140 GiB Pass Download throughput in proxy mode limited by network and storage, not CPU 1.2 GB/s in total with each replica using 0.35 of its 2 CPUs Pass Web replica start to ready under 5 seconds 0.85 to 1.61 s Pass Dataset Viewer /rows p99 under 200 ms on a 10 million row Split p99 16.1 and 27.8 ms at 50 requests per second Pass 100,000 Repos per Instance Repo listings on Postgres: Arsenal page p50 212 ms, Hub list_models with a filter and a sort p50 186 to 244 ms, 12 to 18 queries a request at any size Pass for listings, see Repo listings

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Item Version or value Hangar A pre-release build of 1.0.0 with the performance changes merged as 40ad448, built with make image IMAGE=hangar:bench; baseline runs used commit 382cc88 Host Apple silicon laptop, 12 CPUs, 36 GiB of memory, macOS Containers Docker Desktop 29.8.2 (a Linux VM with 6 vCPUs and 11.7 GiB), Docker Compose 5.6.0 Load generator grafana/k6:1.4.2 in a container limited to 2 CPUs (--cpus 2) Stack deploy/compose/scale.yaml: Traefik v3.6, postgres:18-alpine, MinIO RELEASE.2026-08-04T00-00-00Z, the OpenTelemetry Collector 0.161.0 Web replicas 2, each limited to 2 CPUs and 1 GiB Worker 1 Storage S3 (MinIO), download_mode and upload_mode both proxy Seed data loadtest/seed.sh with the defaults: loadtest/many-files (100,000 files) and loadtest/many-commits (10,000 Commits, checked with git rev-list --count), plus loadtest/resolve; a 10 million row dataset loadtest/rows10m

The limits came from a Compose override file next to scale.yaml:

services:
  traefik:
    command: !override
      - --providers.docker=true
      - --providers.docker.exposedbydefault=false
      - --entrypoints.web.address=:18480
      - --entrypoints.web.transport.respondingTimeouts.readTimeout=0
      - --entrypoints.web.transport.respondingTimeouts.writeTimeout=0
    ports: !override
      - "18480:18480"
  web:
    deploy:
      replicas: 2
      resources:
        limits: {cpus: "2", memory: 1g}
  worker:
    deploy:
      replicas: 1

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Start the stack with the override and the image built from that commit:

HANGAR_IMAGE=hangar:bench HANGAR_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:18480 \
  docker compose -p hangar-bench --env-file .env -f deploy/compose/scale.yaml -f override.yaml up -d

Seed as loadtest/README.md describes, with a write Token for a loadtest user:

HANGAR_URL=http://localhost:18480 HANGAR_TOKEN=hgr_... HANGAR_USERNAME=loadtest loadtest/seed.sh

Run each scenario with k6 in Traefik's network namespace, so localhost:18480 is the same public URL inside and outside the container:

docker run --rm -i --cpus 2 --network container:hangar-bench-traefik-1 \
  -v "$PWD/loadtest:/lt:ro" -w /lt grafana/k6:1.4.2 run \
  -e HANGAR_URL=http://localhost:18480 -e HANGAR_TOKEN=hgr_... \
  -e HANGAR_NAMESPACE=loadtest -e HANGAR_USERNAME=loadtest -e REPLICAS=2 resolve.js

HANGAR_IMAGE and HANGAR_PUBLIC_URL are read by Docker Compose, and HANGAR_URL, HANGAR_TOKEN, HANGAR_USERNAME and HANGAR_NAMESPACE by the load test scripts. They are not Hangar configuration keys, so do not set them where hangar runs: it refuses to start when it sees a HANGAR_ variable it does not know.

The same command ran model_info.js, tree.js, git_clone.js, upload.js (VUS=4, 1 GiB each), download.js (VUS=4, DURATION=2m, after upload.js) and viewer_rows.js (50 requests per second). Memory came from each replica's cgroup (memory.current, memory.peak and memory.stat), sampled every few seconds, and docker stats. CPU per request came from each container's cgroup cpu.stat before and after a run, divided by the requests k6 sent.

docs.title: HEAD /resolve
docs.text:
400 requests per second in total (200 per replica) for 2 minutes, four HEADs for every GET.

Run Host load (1 minute) HEAD p99 All requests p95 Median Final, host busy, 1 43 205.65 ms 57.08 ms 4.67 ms Final, host busy, 2 54 86.99 ms 25.61 ms 4.26 ms Final, host busy, 3 37 103.98 ms 26.38 ms 4.39 ms Final, host quiet, 1 9 12.09 ms 12.54 ms 1.64 ms Final, host quiet, 2 13 12.46 ms 12.59 ms 1.74 ms Final, host quiet, 3 14 6.94 ms 12.23 ms 1.40 ms Final, host quiet, 4 8 27.88 ms 13.20 ms 1.98 ms Baseline 382cc88, host quiet, 1 9 25.40 ms 14.62 ms 2.77 ms Baseline 382cc88, host quiet, 2 11 9.09 ms 13.58 ms 2.25 ms

The tail tracks the load on the host, not Hangar: with other projects' builds and clusters pushing the laptop's load average to 40 to 140, no version met the target, and with the load average near 10, both did. The first baseline run, at a load average of 45, had 1,600 requests time out after 30 seconds; no later run had a failed request.

The database work per download fell. A HEAD /resolve with a Token ran 14 queries at 382cc88 and runs 8 now (TestHubDownloadQueries):

CPU per request, 60-second runs Postgres Each web replica Baseline, host busy (3 runs) 2.69 to 3.02 ms 1.59 to 1.71 ms Final, host busy (4 runs) 1.77 to 1.91 ms 1.32 to 1.46 ms Baseline, host quiet (2 runs) 1.28 to 1.78 ms 0.96 to 1.19 ms Final, host quiet (1 run) 1.14 ms 0.96 ms

docs.title: Model info
docs.text: 100 requests per second for 2 minutes, half /api/models/{repo} and half /revision/main: p99 62.73, 29.40 and 19.30 ms with the host busy (load average 34 to 44), and 12.52 ms with it quiet. No failed requests.

docs.title: Tree listing
docs.text: Four clients listing all 100,000 files of many-files for 2 minutes, 101 pages each: p95 6.45 and 6.79 s with the host busy, 6.15 s with it quiet. Every listing returned every file.

docs.title: Clone
docs.text: Four clients cloning many-commits (4.4 MB pack) for 3 minutes, in five runs: p95 995.59 ms, 1.13 s and 829.95 ms with the host busy, 599 ms with it quiet. The fifth run, with the host busy, is the one in Clone errors; its p95 was not kept with the results, so it is not listed here or in the summary.

docs.title: Clone errors
docs.text:
One busy run had 2 of 904 pack responses end early: k6 reported unexpected EOF, and the replica logged git upload-pack ended early with context canceled, which means the connection from Traefik closed first. That run failed its http_req_failed threshold (0.11% against 0.1%). The other four clone runs, the ones listed in Clone, had none in about 3,900 clones, and nothing in Hangar's logs explains the closed connections. Treat it as unexplained until it happens on a quiet host.

During clones, a replica's memory peaked at 285 and 496 MiB, mostly the git upload-pack and pack-objects processes in its cgroup, under the 1 GiB limit. The 256 MiB target covers uploads and downloads of files, not git clones.

docs.title: Uploads
docs.text: Four concurrent 1 GiB uploads through the native upload API (16 MiB parts, proxied to MinIO): every plan, part, completion and Commit succeeded, 1 minute 32 seconds per object on average. Each replica's cgroup peaked at 66 and 81 MiB (of which about 20 MiB was the Go heap and the rest page cache and /tmp files), and stayed between 35 and 66 MiB through the run.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text: Four clients downloading a 1 GiB file through /resolve for 2 minutes, bodies discarded: 140 downloads, 140 GiB, 1.2 GB/s in total. Each replica peaked at 104 and 115 MiB, and used 42 CPU-seconds in 122 seconds, 0.35 of its 2 CPUs. Traefik used 91 CPU-seconds, more than either replica, so the replicas were not what limited the throughput.

docs.title: Start to ready
docs.text: Five times, a stopped web replica was started with docker start while a container on the Compose network polled its /readyz every 50 ms: 1.61, 0.94, 0.85, 1.41 and 1.50 seconds to the first 200. The times include starting the polling container, so they overstate the replica's own start.

docs.title: Dataset Viewer rows
docs.text: viewer_rows.js against a 10 million row Parquet Split (184 MB, three columns), 50 requests per second for 2 minutes, 100 rows from a random offset each: p99 27.77 and 16.11 ms, median 9.28 and 8.54 ms, every response the requested rows. The in-process load test (go test -tags load -run TestLoadRows ./internal/datasets/viewer) measured p99 1.89 ms on the same machine.

docs.title: Repo listings
docs.text: The Arsenal page asks the native API for a page of Repos with facet counts, and the Hub's /api/models and /api/datasets take filters such as filter=library:transformers and sorts by downloads and likes. Until this change, each of these read every Repo the caller could see, with two to four queries per Repo, and then each Repo on the page cost 4 to 15 more queries. Now the Repo service keeps each Repo's facets in the repo_facts and repo_facet_values tables, which triggers mark out of date when a ref, index result, Split size or setting changes, and filters, sorts, pages and counts facets in SQL. A page's heads, index results, scan statuses, likes, downloads and the caller's Roles are read with one or two queries each.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
TestLoadListing (cmd/hangar/listing_load_test.go, build tag load) runs the whole server in the test process: authentication, the native API, the Hub API and the Repo service. It writes N Repos straight into the database, so the sizes it reaches are not limited by how fast git creates Repos:

  • 100 Organisations and the caller's own Namespace; the caller belongs to 5 of the Organisations.
  • 70% public, 15% internal and 15% private Repos; 80% models and 20% datasets.
  • Every Repo has a branch head, a Commit row, a scan result and index results shaped like real ones: transformers models with four safetensors files, a config and card data; GGUF models with two to seven quantisations and a chat template; datasets with Parquet files, a language, a task and a size category.
  • A third of the Repos have between 1 and 19 likes and downloads on 10 of the last 60 days.

Each request carries a read Token of a user who is not an admin. For each scenario the test sends one request, then 20 timed ones (5 at 100,000 Repos, and 1 for the Postgres baseline at 100,000 Repos, where one request took more than a minute), and counts the queries each runs with a bun query hook:

Scenario Request Arsenal page GET /api/hangar/v1/repos?limit=60 Arsenal with a filter and a sort GET /api/hangar/v1/repos?limit=60&library=transformers&sort=downloads Hub, filter and sort GET /api/models?filter=library:transformers&sort=downloads&limit=100 Hub, likes sort GET /api/models?sort=likes&limit=100 
go test -tags load -run TestLoadListing -timeout 60m -v ./cmd/hangar
HANGAR_LOAD_REPOS=100000 go test -tags load -run TestLoadListing -timeout 60m -v ./cmd/hangar
HANGAR_TEST_POSTGRES=1 HANGAR_LOAD_DRIVER=postgres HANGAR_LOAD_REPOS=1000,10000,100000 \
  go test -tags load -run TestLoadListing -timeout 120m -v ./cmd/hangar

HANGAR_LOAD_RUNS sets the number of timed requests, and HANGAR_LOAD_TRACE=1 logs the slowest queries of each scenario. The baseline is 1d42e93 (v1.2.3) with the same test files added. Both ran on the laptop in Setup, with Go 1.27.3, SQLite in a temporary folder and Postgres 18 (postgres:18-alpine with fsync=off, as the test suite runs it) in Docker Desktop, with nothing else running. Each query to Postgres in Docker Desktop costs about 0.4 ms in round trips, which is most of the baseline's time on Postgres.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Postgres, the database the 100,000 Repo target is for. Median latency, then queries per request:

Scenario Repos Before After Arsenal page 1,000 987 ms, 3,109 queries 15 ms, 18 queries Arsenal page 10,000 5.79 s, 20,138 queries 32 ms, 18 queries Arsenal page 100,000 74.7 s, 189,883 queries 212 ms, 18 queries Arsenal with a filter and a sort 1,000 1.34 s, 4,808 queries 22 ms, 17 queries Arsenal with a filter and a sort 10,000 11.5 s, 37,271 queries 44 ms, 17 queries Arsenal with a filter and a sort 100,000 134.7 s, 361,517 queries 493 ms, 17 queries Hub, filter and sort 1,000 888 ms, 3,372 queries 31 ms, 12 queries Hub, filter and sort 10,000 8.85 s, 27,820 queries 22 ms, 12 queries Hub, filter and sort 100,000 102.4 s, 275,781 queries 186 ms, 12 queries Hub, likes sort 1,000 1.00 s, 3,372 queries 12 ms, 12 queries Hub, likes sort 10,000 6.54 s, 27,820 queries 22 ms, 12 queries Hub, likes sort 100,000 119.2 s, 275,781 queries 244 ms, 12 queries

SQLite:

Scenario Repos Before After Arsenal page 1,000 75 ms, 3,109 queries 16 ms, 18 queries Arsenal page 10,000 567 ms, 20,138 queries 93 ms, 18 queries Arsenal page 100,000 8.34 s, 189,883 queries 1.13 s, 18 queries Arsenal with a filter and a sort 1,000 107 ms, 4,808 queries 12 ms, 17 queries Arsenal with a filter and a sort 10,000 1.08 s, 37,271 queries 71 ms, 17 queries Arsenal with a filter and a sort 100,000 15.3 s, 361,516 queries 666 ms, 17 queries Hub, filter and sort 1,000 75 ms, 3,372 queries 12 ms, 12 queries Hub, filter and sort 10,000 755 ms, 27,820 queries 32 ms, 12 queries Hub, filter and sort 100,000 9.14 s, 275,780 queries 188 ms, 12 queries Hub, likes sort 1,000 76 ms, 3,372 queries 13 ms, 12 queries Hub, likes sort 10,000 844 ms, 27,820 queries 34 ms, 12 queries Hub, likes sort 100,000 8.29 s, 275,780 queries 153 ms, 12 queries

TestListingQueriesDoNotGrowWithRepos (cmd/hangar/listing_queries_test.go) keeps the query counts the same at 40 and 440 Repos, and TestListingPagesMatchReadingEachRepo (cmd/hangar/listing_pages_test.go) and TestListFactsMatchReadingEveryRepo (internal/repo/listfacts_test.go) check that the answers, facet counts and cursors are the same as before.

The first listing after Repos are created or change rebuilds their repo_facts rows, 500 Repos at a time. Building rows for 100,000 new Repos took 28.3 s on Postgres and 39.8 s on SQLite, once. After an upgrade, workers build them on start, and the worker leader rebuilds rows that are out of date every minute, so listings seldom have rows to build.

At 100,000 Repos, what is left is work in the database that grows with the Repos the caller can see: counting facet values (about 120 ms on Postgres and 700 ms on SQLite for the Arsenal page) and sorting by downloads or likes, which sums each visible Repo's downloads or likes (about 200 to 300 ms on Postgres).

docs.title: Sign-in burst
docs.text: Not one of the targets, but found while measuring memory: 40 parallel failed sign-ins (POST /api/hangar/v1/auth/login) took the baseline's replicas to their 1 GiB limit, and the kernel killed one. Each password check holds 64 MiB (argon2id), and nothing limited how many ran at once. With password hashing limited to two at a time per process (one on a 2 CPU replica), the same burst finished in 5 seconds and each replica peaked at 209 MiB.

docs.title: Deviations
docs.text:
• One machine. k6 ran on the same host as Hangar, in a container limited to 2 CPUs, not on a second machine. The Docker VM had 6 vCPUs for the two replicas (4 CPUs of limits), Postgres, MinIO, Traefik, the worker and k6.
  • A shared host. Other projects' containers, builds and a kind cluster ran on the laptop and in the same Docker VM throughout. The laptop's load average ranged from 8 to 144 and the VM's from 2 to 8. Each result above gives the load it ran under; scenarios were repeated to separate noise from regressions.
  • Traefik's port. Traefik listened on 18480 inside its container, so k6 could share its network namespace and follow the Link headers Hangar writes with its public URL.
  • 50 GiB transfers. The laptop's disk had too little room for a 50 GiB upload, so uploads were 4 × 1 GiB. Downloads repeated a 1 GiB file to 140 GiB in total.
  • Upload Repos. upload.js commits each VU's file to its own Repo. With all four on one branch, a Commit could get 409 when its three retries ran out, which was then the specified behaviour for Commits without a parent Commit, not what this scenario measures. Since 2026-10-18, such Commits wait a jittered, growing time between up to seven retries (the specification's Git chapter, "Server-side Commits"); TestConcurrentCommitsToOneBranch (internal/repo/commit_test.go) covers eight at once. The load test was not run again with one branch, so the numbers above are unchanged.
  • Rows dataset. seed.sh does not create the 10 million row dataset; it was generated with PyArrow (columns n int64, s string, f float64) and pushed with git LFS.
  • Repo listings in process. The Repo listings results come from an in-process load test on SQLite and on Postgres in Docker Desktop, not from k6 against deploy/compose/scale.yaml, and cover listings only: the other scenarios ran with a few Repos, not 100,000.
  • Not measured. The /filter target in the Dataset Viewer chapter, which only the in-process load test covers.

docs.title: Is Hangar a model registry?
docs.text:
It covers the storage and serving side of one. Hangar is a self-hosted model and dataset hub: every Repo is a git repository with branches, tags and Commits, and clients load files through the Hugging Face Hub API, git, Ollama or LM Studio.

For experiment tracking and model lineage, pair it with MLflow: MLflow records runs and model versions, and Hangar stores and serves the files. See How Hangar compares.

docs.title: Is Hangar a private Hugging Face Hub alternative?
docs.text: Yes. Hangar serves the Hugging Face Hub API from your own servers and storage, so models and datasets stay on your network. Set HF_ENDPOINT to your Instance, and huggingface_hub, transformers and datasets use it in place of huggingface.co. Private Repos are visible only to the Users and Organisations you give access. See Point HF_ENDPOINT at Hangar. For what Hugging Face itself offers, see Hugging Face Hub on-premises.

docs.title: Is Hangar a cache for Hugging Face models?
docs.text:
It does more than cache. Each Pull keeps a Mirror of the Repo with its git history and the upstream Commit SHAs, so a Revision pinned in your code still resolves after the upstream Repo changes or disappears. You can also upload models that exist nowhere else. Clients load everything from your own storage.

A caching proxy, such as olah, keeps whatever clients happen to download. How Hangar compares sets the two kinds of tool side by side.

docs.title: Does Hangar run models?
docs.text: No. Hangar stores and serves files. Run models with the tools you already use, such as transformers, vLLM, Ollama or LM Studio, and point them at Hangar for the weights. Spaces, the Inference API, Hugging Face Jobs, Buckets and kernels, SSH git and Xet downloads are out of scope.

docs.title: Is there a hosted version?
docs.text: No. Hangar is self-hosted only, and its licence does not let others offer it as a hosted or managed service. To look around without installing anything, open the demo: it runs on sample data, and nothing you do there is saved.

docs.title: Do I need to change my code?
docs.text: No. Set HF_ENDPOINT to your Instance and HF_TOKEN to a Token you create in Hangar. huggingface_hub, the hf CLI, transformers, diffusers, sentence-transformers, datasets and vLLM then work unchanged. Code that names a Repo, such as org/model, and a Revision keeps working, because Mirrors keep the upstream IDs and Commit SHAs.

docs.title: Which versions of my tools work?
docs.text: Tested versions and platforms lists the versions of huggingface_hub, Python, transformers, git, Ollama, Postgres and Kubernetes that CI runs against, and what is documented but not tested. Hub API compatibility lists every Hub endpoint and whether Hangar serves it.

docs.title: Does it work with Ollama and LM Studio?
docs.text: Yes. ollama pull hangar.example.com/org/model:Q4_K_M pulls a GGUF quantisation straight from your Instance, and hangar lmstudio install org/model:Q4_K_M puts one into LM Studio's models folder. See Ollama and LM Studio. To serve GGUF models to every Ollama install on your network, see Run a private Ollama registry.

docs.title: Does it work with hf_xet?
docs.text: Yes for uploads. Hangar accepts Xet uploads, so huggingface_hub with hf_xet installed works with no setup. It stores whole files and serves them over plain HTTP.

docs.title: Does it handle datasets?
docs.text: Yes. Dataset Repos work with load_dataset, pandas and Polars over hf:// and DuckDB over HTTPS, and the web UI has a Dataset Viewer. Hangar builds a Parquet export of each dataset, as huggingface.co does. See Datasets.

docs.title: Can Hangar run air-gapped, with no internet access?
docs.text: Yes. An Instance with no internet access pulls from another Hangar Instance that has it, as its Upstream. You can also carry a backup or a Hugging Face cache across and import it. See Air-gapped Instances.

docs.title: What does it need to run?
docs.text: One container, or one binary with git 2.39 or later, and disk space for the models you keep. It scales out to several processes over Postgres and S3-compatible storage. See System requirements.

docs.title: Does Hangar connect to anything on the internet?
docs.text:
Only to what you configure. The server connects to its database and Blob store, to Upstreams when someone pulls or a tracking Mirror checks for new Commits, to OIDC providers when people sign in, to webhook targets, and to an OpenTelemetry endpoint if you set one. huggingface.co is a built-in Upstream; turn it off with upstreams.huggingface.enabled: false. Hangar sends no usage data anywhere.

In the browser, the web UI links to these docs at https://hangar.page/ (change or remove the links with ui.docs_url), and Model cards load images from other sites unless an admin turns off Load external images in cards under Admin, Settings.

docs.title: What happens to my data if I stop using Hangar?
docs.text: It stays usable without Hangar. Every Repo is a git repository, and large files are stored whole, under their SHA-256, in your folder or bucket, so you can copy them out with standard tools. See Where Hangar keeps data and Uninstall Hangar.

docs.title: How do I upgrade, and which versions get fixes?
docs.text: Pin a version, back up, then follow Upgrades. Security fixes go into the latest minor release; see Versioning and support.

docs.title: Where do I get help?
docs.text: Check hangar admin doctor and Troubleshooting first, then open a GitHub issue. See Get help.

docs.title: Is Hangar open source?
docs.text: No, Hangar is source-available. The code is public on GitHub under the Elastic License 2.0, and you can read it, change it and self-host it for free, including inside your company. The licence is not OSI-approved open source because it stops others from offering Hangar as a hosted or managed service.

docs.title: What does it cost?
docs.text: Nothing. Hangar is source-available under the Elastic License 2.0. You can use, change and self-host it, including inside your company. You can't offer it to others as a hosted or managed service, or remove licence notices.

docs.title: Can my company use it?
docs.text: Yes, for free, on your own infrastructure. The limits are the ones above: you can't offer Hangar to others as a hosted or managed service, or remove licence notices. For anything else, read the licence itself; this FAQ is not legal advice.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: The words Hangar uses, in its UI, API and these docs.

docs.title: The Instance
docs.text: Term Meaning Instance One running deployment of Hangar: one or more server and worker processes sharing a database and a Blob store. Arsenal Everything stored in an Instance that you can see. The UI lists it in two sections, Models and Datasets. Namespace The owner part of a Repo ID: a User or an Organisation. Names are unique across both. User A person who signs in, locally or through OIDC. Every User has a personal Namespace. Organisation A Namespace that Users join as Members with a Role. Role A Member's permission level in an Organisation: read, write or admin. See Permissions. Token A secret that a client presents as a bearer token or git password, with a scope and an optional expiry. See Permissions.

docs.title: Content
docs.text: Term Meaning Repo A versioned set of files, of type model or dataset, with an ID namespace/name. Every Repo is a git repository. See Repos and Revisions. Revision Anything that names a Commit: a branch, a tag or a Commit SHA. Commit A real git commit in a Repo. Commit SHAs are git SHA-1 values, as on the Hugging Face Hub. LFS object A large file's content, stored once per Instance and addressed by its SHA-256. git trees hold a pointer file instead. Blob store Where LFS objects and git data live: a local folder or an S3-compatible bucket. See Storage backends. Model card A Repo's README.md, with optional YAML front matter. Collection A named, ordered list of Repos that a Namespace curates. See Collections.

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text: Term Meaning Config A named subset of a dataset Repo, from the card's configs: YAML or inferred from its file layout. Split A named part of a Config, such as train or test. Parquet export Parquet files of every Config and Split, on the refs/convert/parquet branch. Dataset Viewer The service that previews, searches, filters and summarises dataset rows, with an API compatible with the Hub's. See Datasets.

docs.title: Getting models and datasets in
docs.text: Term Meaning Upstream Another Hugging Face-compatible hub Hangar can fetch from, such as huggingface.co or another Hangar Instance. See Mirrors and Upstreams. Mirror A Repo that tracks a Repo on an Upstream, keeping its ID and Commit SHAs. A tracking Mirror's check for new upstream Commits is a Mirror sync. Partial mirror A Mirror with the full git history but only some LFS objects, such as one GGUF quantisation. Files it does not hold are not present. Pull Fetching a Repo, or some of its files, from an Upstream into the Arsenal. See Pulls and Dependencies. Pull-through An optional mode where a client's request for a Repo that is not in the Arsenal starts a Pull automatically. Dependency A link from one Repo to another it needs (code) or builds on (a base model). Discover The UI view that searches Upstreams and marks what is already in the Arsenal.

docs.title: Work and events
docs.text: Term Meaning Job Background work, such as a Pull, indexing or garbage collection. See Jobs. index Metadata Hangar reads from a Commit's files: formats, architecture, parameter count, quantisation, context length and licence. scan A security check on a Commit's files, such as finding dangerous imports in pickle files. See Security hardening. webhook An HTTP callback that a Namespace or Repo admin registers for events. See Webhooks.

docs.title: How Hangar compares
docs.text:
Teams that want models and datasets on their own infrastructure usually look at one of three kinds of tool: a caching proxy in front of huggingface.co, a full self-hosted hub, or an MLOps model registry. Hangar is a self-hosted hub: it serves the Hugging Face Hub API, keeps Mirrors with their git history, and also accepts your own uploads.

This page compares Hangar with tools people evaluate alongside it. Each fact about another tool comes from that tool's own documentation or source code, linked in Sources: MatrixHub, KohakuHub and ModnFace were checked on 21 October 2026, and the others on 20 October 2026. Tools change, so check their current documentation before you decide.

docs.text:

docs.title: Caching proxies: olah, Artifactory and Nexus
docs.text:
A caching proxy sits in front of huggingface.co and keeps a copy of what clients download. It is the smallest change for teams that only need faster or controlled downloads.

  • olah is a lightweight mirror server. It caches files block by block as clients ask for them, and an offline mode serves only what is already cached. It has no upload routes.
  • JFrog Artifactory has remote Hugging Face repositories that cache huggingface.co, and local repositories you can upload to with upload_folder. It suits organisations that already run Artifactory for other package types.
  • Sonatype Nexus Repository supports Hugging Face as a proxy repository for models and datasets. It has no hosted Hugging Face repositories, so you cannot upload to it.

Choose Hangar over a proxy when you want Mirrors that keep the upstream git history and Commit SHAs, so a model pinned to a Commit still resolves after upstream changes, or when you also need uploads, git, Ollama or LM Studio.

docs.title: Self-hosted hubs: MatrixHub, KohakuHub and CSGHub
docs.text:
These serve the Hub API from your own infrastructure and accept uploads, as Hangar does.

  • MatrixHub is a self-hosted model hub aimed at serving models to inference engines such as vLLM, SGLang and Dynamo inside a company network. Repositories live in projects. A proxy project caches a model from huggingface.co, or another registry, the first time a client asks for it, and admins can also pull or push models between registries, including other MatrixHub instances, by hand or on a schedule. It handles models only; dataset support is on its roadmap. It runs with Docker Compose on SQLite, or with Helm on MySQL, and stores files on a local volume or NFS; S3-compatible storage is on its roadmap. On 21 October 2026, its latest release was 0.2.0.
  • KohakuHub is a self-hosted Hugging Face Hub alternative for models and datasets, built on LakeFS for versioning, S3-compatible storage such as MinIO, and Postgres or SQLite. When a Repo is not stored locally, it can show the Repo from huggingface.co or another KohakuHub instance and send downloads there, rather than keeping a copy. git clone works; git push is in development. Its README describes it as an alpha. The core is AGPL-3.0, and its Dataset Viewer is under the Kohaku Software License 1.0: free for non-commercial use, with commercial use after a trial needing a paid licence.
  • CSGHub from OpenCSG is a self-hosted hub with a web UI, git access through Gitea, and dataset previews. Admins run mirror tasks that sync whole Repos from upstream hubs.

Hangar differs in scope: it serves GGUF models straight to Ollama and LM Studio, pulls only the files you choose, such as one quantisation, as a Partial mirror, keeps the upstream git history and Commit SHAs of every Mirror, and runs as a single binary or container with SQLite, or with Postgres and S3-compatible storage.

ModnFace describes itself, on its GitHub organisation's profile, as a self-hostable alternative to the Hugging Face Hub built on Hugging Face's own open-source components, with Xet storage, Spaces and air-gapped deployment. On 21 October 2026 the organisation published forks of other projects, such as huggingface_hub, xet-core and transformers, but no server code, installation guide or licence for ModnFace itself. Its features cannot be checked, so it is not in the table.

docs.title: Model registries: MLflow
docs.text:
MLflow Model Registry tracks model versions, aliases and lineage for models you train and log with MLflow. It does not serve the Hugging Face Hub API, so huggingface_hub, transformers and HF_ENDPOINT do not work with it.

The two can work together: MLflow for experiment tracking and model lineage, and Hangar to store the weights and serve them to Hugging Face clients, git, Ollama and LM Studio.

docs.title: Hugging Face Team and Enterprise
docs.text:
Hugging Face's paid plans add organisation features such as single sign-on, audit logs and a choice of US or EU storage regions. The plans page does not offer a self-hosted or on-premises option, so the files stay on huggingface.co.

Choose Hangar when the files must stay on your own servers or network, including air-gapped networks. Hugging Face Hub on-premises explains what Hugging Face offers and what a self-hosted Hub has to do.

docs.title: What Hangar does not do
docs.text: Hangar stores and serves files; it does not run models. Spaces, the Inference API, Hugging Face Jobs, Buckets and kernels, SSH git and Xet downloads are out of scope. For the Hub API endpoints Hangar serves, see Hub API compatibility.

docs.title: On the server
docs.text:
What Default location Holds The database database.dsn: /var/lib/hangar/hangar.db with SQLite, or your Postgres database Everything except file contents: Repos and their refs, users, Organisations, Tokens (as hashes), settings, Jobs, sessions and the audit log. SQLite also keeps a lock file next to it, hangar.db.lock. The Blob store storage.fs.path: /var/lib/hangar/blobs, or a bucket LFS objects, git data and upload staging. See the layout below. secrets.yaml server.data_dir: /var/lib/hangar The Instance key and the first admin's password, if Hangar generated them on first start. Mode 0600. The git pack cache git.cache_dir: /var/cache/hangar/git Copies of git packs for Repos in use. Disposable: delete it whenever Hangar is stopped. Temporary files TMPDIR: /tmp in the image Upload parts while they are sent to S3, deleted when each part is done.

In the container image, /var/lib/hangar is the volume, and /var/cache/hangar and /tmp can be a tmpfs.

The Instance key encrypts the secrets Hangar stores in the database, such as users' Upstream tokens, the Instance's token for each Upstream and webhook secrets, and signs the URLs Hangar hands out. Without it, a restored database cannot decrypt them. Keep it with your backups, but not in the same place; see Backup and restore.

docs.title: The Blob store layout
docs.text:
The keys are the same on the filesystem and on S3, under storage.s3.prefix if you set one:

Key Holds lfs/sha256/<first 2>/<next 2>/<sha256> Each LFS object, whole and unchanged, named by its SHA-256. One copy per Instance, however many Repos hold it. git/<Repo UUID>/pack/ Each Repo's git packs. The Repo's branches and tags are in the database. xet/xorbs/ Data that hf_xet uploads, kept for xet.xorb_retention (28 days) after its last use so later uploads can skip it. exports/ Zip exports of Repo folders. uploads/, tmp/ Uploads in progress: the parts of multipart uploads on the filesystem backend, and uploads staged under tmp/uploads/ before Hangar checks them.

hangar admin backup copies every key except uploads/, tmp/ and exports/.

docs.title: On your machine
docs.text:
The hangar CLI and the tools it drives keep these:

What Where Holds CLI settings ~/.config/hangar/config.yaml, or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/hangar/ The Instance URL and your username. The Token too, with mode 0600, when no OS keychain is available. The Token The OS keychain, under the service name hangar and the Instance URL The Token hangar login saved. LM Studio installs ~/.config/hangar/lmstudio.json, and links in LM Studio's models folder What hangar lmstudio install put into LM Studio, so list and remove can find it. Downloaded files The Hugging Face cache: $HF_HUB_CACHE, ~/.cache/huggingface/hub by default Files hangar pull downloads, in the layout Python libraries read. The cache is shared with every Hugging Face tool, not Hangar's own. Your Ollama key ~/.ollama/id_ed25519.pub Ollama's own key. hangar ollama key register sends the public half to the Instance, which lists it under Settings, Ollama keys.

docs.title: Getting your files out
docs.text:
While Hangar runs, git clone gets a Repo with its full history and LFS files, and hf download or hangar pull gets its files; see git and git-lfs.

Without Hangar running, every large file is still whole in the Blob store at lfs/sha256/..., under the SHA-256 that its LFS pointer names, so standard tools can copy it out. A hangar admin backup folder holds the same objects under blobs/, and every database table as JSON lines under db/. To move to another Instance or backend, back up and restore; to remove Hangar, see Uninstall Hangar.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
Background work runs as Jobs in the database-backed queue: Pulls (pull, pull.file), Mirror syncs, indexing and scanning, garbage collection, git compaction, Parquet exports and dataset statistics, webhook deliveries, zip exports and purges.

  • Workers claim Jobs with a lease, renewed while they run. If a worker dies, its Jobs go back to the queue when the lease expires, and they resume where they stopped.
  • The same work is never queued twice: pulling the same files twice joins the existing Job.
  • Pulls report bytes done, the total, the rate and an ETA, per file and overall.

See your Jobs under Jobs in the UI, or with the CLI:

hangar jobs list
hangar jobs watch <job-id>
hangar jobs cancel <job-id>

Admins see every Job. Processes in role all or worker run Jobs; web processes only queue them. See Scaling.

docs.title: Upstreams
docs.text:
An Upstream is a hub that speaks the Hugging Face Hub API. huggingface.co is built in, with the ID huggingface. Admins can add others, such as another Hangar Instance or a corporate mirror, under Admin, Upstreams, and turn any of them off.

Requests to an Upstream use your own upstream token if you saved one (Settings, Upstream tokens), otherwise the Instance token configured for that Upstream, otherwise none.

An Upstream can be on your local network, such as another Hangar Instance on the LAN. Hangar connects to an Upstream's own host wherever it is, but follows a redirect to a private address only when the Upstream's own host is private too, so huggingface.co or another public Upstream cannot point Hangar at services inside your network. Hangar never connects to link-local or cloud metadata addresses. If Hangar reaches Upstreams through a proxy (HTTPS_PROXY), the proxy decides which addresses it can reach.

docs.title: Mirrors keep upstream IDs
docs.text:
A Pull of jinaai/jina-embeddings-v3 creates the Repo jinaai/jina-embeddings-v3 in Hangar, with the same Commit SHAs. That is what makes HF_ENDPOINT a drop-in swap.

  • The first Pull into an unknown Namespace creates it as an Organisation owned by the Instance. Admins can hand it to a user or Organisation later.
  • If a local Namespace already has the name, the Pull fails unless the admin sets a prefix for that Upstream (upstreams.<id>.namespace_prefix, such as hf-). Prefixed Mirrors such as hf-jinaai/jina-embeddings-v3 no longer work as drop-in replacements.
  • Mirrors are read-only to git push and the commit API, so they stay identical to the Upstream. A Namespace admin can detach a Mirror, which turns it into an ordinary Repo that keeps its history.

docs.title: Partial mirrors
docs.text: A Partial mirror has the full git history but only some LFS objects, for example one GGUF quantisation. Files that are not held show as Not in arsenal in the UI and the CLI, and you can pull them later.

docs.title: Tracking
docs.text: A Mirror can follow its upstream branch (--track on hangar pull, or Track upstream in the UI). It then checks for new Commits on a schedule, six-hourly by default, and pulls new versions of the files it already selected. A GGUF quant selection follows the quant, not a file name, so a renamed file of the same quant is still followed. Commits replaced by an upstream force-push stay reachable under refs/hangar/previous/<time>, so nothing pinned to them breaks.

docs.title: Pull-through
docs.text: Pull-through is off by default. When it is on (pull.pull_through.enabled) and a Repo ID matches pull.pull_through.allow, a Hub API or git request for a Repo that is not in the Arsenal starts a Pull automatically, and a download of a file that is not present starts that file's Pull and streams it as it arrives.

  • Air-gapped Instances: use another Hangar Instance as the Upstream.

docs.title: Hugging Face Hub on-premises
docs.text: Hugging Face does not offer the Hugging Face Hub as software you run on your own servers. Its plans page lists no such option, and it stopped offering on-premises deployments of its Private Hub in 2023. Its Team and Enterprise plans add organisation features to huggingface.co, and your files stay there. To keep models and datasets on your own infrastructure and still use the Hugging Face tools, you run a self-hosted hub that serves the same API, such as Hangar.

docs.title: What Hugging Face offers
docs.text:
Hugging Face's Team and Enterprise plans add single sign-on, audit logs, Token management and a choice of US or EU storage regions to an organisation on huggingface.co. The plans page does not list a self-hosted or on-premises option.

In August 2022, Hugging Face announced a Private Hub with managed, customer-cloud and on-premises deployments. A June 2023 update to that announcement says the on-premises deployments are no longer offered, and that the Private Hub is now called Enterprise Hub.

docs.title: What an on-premises Hub needs to do
docs.text:
The Hugging Face libraries do not need huggingface.co itself. They need a server that answers the Hub API the way huggingface.co does. huggingface_hub reads the server's address from HF_ENDPOINT, and transformers, datasets, sentence-transformers, diffusers, vLLM and the hf CLI all download through it. For code to work unchanged, a self-hosted Hub has to:

  • Serve the Hub API endpoints the clients call, including file downloads at a Revision, file listings, Repo metadata and, for uploads, the commit API.
  • Keep the same Repo IDs and Commit SHAs as huggingface.co for models you copy from there, so code that pins a Revision keeps working.
  • Store large files the way clients expect, and accept uploads from huggingface_hub, including Xet uploads from hf_xet, which recent versions install by default.
  • Check Tokens and decide who can read and write each Repo.

docs.title: How Hangar provides it
docs.text:
Hangar is a self-hosted model and dataset hub, compatible with the Hugging Face Hub API, git, Ollama and LM Studio. It runs on your servers, from one container with SQLite and a local folder to replicas over Postgres and S3-compatible storage. Clients set HF_ENDPOINT and HF_TOKEN, and their code does not change.

On huggingface.co In Hangar Models and datasets in Repos with git history Repos, each a real git repository, with the same Commit SHAs for Mirrors of huggingface.co Repos Downloading from huggingface.co Pulls from huggingface.co or another Instance, of whole Repos or selected files such as one GGUF quant, and optional Pull-through Private and gated Repos Private Repos and gated models, with Organisations, Roles and Token scopes; see Permissions Single sign-on OIDC with providers such as Keycloak, Microsoft Entra ID, Okta and Google Audit logs An audit log of security-relevant actions, exported with OpenTelemetry Storage regions Your own storage: a local folder or any S3-compatible bucket; see Storage backends The Dataset Viewer A Dataset Viewer with an API compatible with the Hub's; see Datasets ollama pull hf.co/... ollama pull from your Instance; see Ollama

Hangar's CI runs huggingface_hub, the hf CLI, transformers, sentence-transformers and datasets against it on every pull request. Hub API compatibility lists every Hub endpoint and whether Hangar serves it, and Tested versions and platforms lists the versions.

docs.title: Connected or air-gapped
docs.text: An Instance with internet access pulls from huggingface.co when someone asks for a model, and serves it from your storage after that. An Instance with no internet access can pull from another Instance that has it, or be filled from a backup or a Hugging Face cache carried across. See Air-gapped Instances.

docs.title: What stays on huggingface.co
docs.text: Hangar stores and serves files; it does not run models. Spaces, the Inference API, Hugging Face Jobs, Buckets and kernels are out of scope. So are Xet downloads and SSH git: Hangar serves files over plain HTTP, which every client supports. For the endpoints it serves, see Hub API compatibility.

docs.title: Licence
docs.text: Hangar is source-available under the Elastic License 2.0. You can use, change and self-host it, including inside your company, for free. You can't offer it to others as a hosted or managed service.

docs.title: Other self-hosted options
docs.text: Hangar is one of several ways to keep Hugging Face models on your own infrastructure. Caching proxies such as JFrog Artifactory and Sonatype Nexus, and other self-hosted hubs such as MatrixHub, are compared in How Hangar compares.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Checked on 23 October 2026:

  • Hugging Face: Team and Enterprise plans
  • Hugging Face: Introducing the Private Hub, published 3 August 2022, with its June 2023 update
  • Hugging Face: Environment variables for HF_ENDPOINT

docs.title: Users, Organisations and Roles
docs.text:
Every User has a personal Namespace. Organisations are Namespaces that Users join as Members with a Role:

Role Can read See the Organisation's private Repos and download from them. write Also create Repos, upload, push and start Pulls into the Organisation. admin Also manage Members, settings, webhooks, and rename, transfer and delete Repos.

A Repo can also have collaborators with read or write, for people outside its Namespace. Instance admins can do everything; the first one is created from configuration (security.bootstrap_admin).

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text:
A Token has one scope, which caps what it can do on top of the user's own permissions:

Scope Can read Download files and read metadata and history. write Also upload, push and start Pulls. On Repos the user administers, also what a write Token does on huggingface.co through huggingface_hub: delete_repo, update_repo_settings (visibility and gating) and move_repo within the same Namespace. admin Also everything else that administers a Repo, such as transfers to another Namespace, webhooks, collaborators, access requests and every setting in the native API and the UI; managing Organisation Members; and, for Instance admins, the Instance.

A Token can be limited to some Namespaces or Repos, and given an expiry. Clients send it as Authorization: Bearer hgr_... over HTTP, or as the password of HTTP Basic credentials, which only git and git-lfs routes accept. Hangar stores only a hash of each Token, and shows when it was last used.

docs.title: Private Repos stay hidden
docs.text: Requests for a private Repo you cannot read get the same answer as a Repo that does not exist (404), as on huggingface.co, so Repo names do not leak.

docs.title: Large files you add by their hash
docs.text: Hangar stores each LFS object once, however many Repos hold it. A Commit can still add a large file by its SHA-256 alone only if you uploaded that file before or can read a Repo that holds it. Otherwise Hangar asks for the bytes, as if it had never seen the file: huggingface_hub, hf and git-lfs send them without you doing anything, and Hangar checks them without storing a second copy. So knowing a file's hash is not enough to get a copy of a file in a private Repo.

docs.title: Gated Repos
docs.text: An admin of a Repo can require people to ask for access, with a form. Admins of the Repo accept or reject requests, automatically or by hand. See Gated models.

docs.title: Ollama keys
docs.text: Ollama signs its registry requests with its own key pair. Register ~/.ollama/id_ed25519.pub under Settings, Ollama keys (or hangar ollama key register) so ollama pull works for Repos that are not public. See Ollama.

docs.title: Your account
docs.text: Under Settings, Profile you can change your display name and email, and your password. A new email takes effect when you open its confirmation link: Hangar sends no mail, so ask an admin to create the link (Admin, Users, Email link) and send it to the new address. Until then your old email stays. To change the password you enter the current one; the new one needs at least 10 characters and cannot be a common password. Changing it signs out your other sessions, keeps this one, and leaves your Tokens working. A Token cannot change a password, but a write Token can change your display name and email (PATCH /api/hangar/v1/me). If you sign in with an OIDC provider and have no Hangar password, change your password with the provider. If you forget your password, ask an admin for a reset link.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.text: Hangar records security-relevant actions, such as sign-ins, password and profile changes, Token changes, Membership changes and visibility changes, in the audit log under Admin, Audit log, and exports them as OpenTelemetry log records.

docs.title: A Pull's lifecycle
docs.text:
A Pull names an Upstream, a Repo, a Revision (the upstream default branch if you give none) and a file selection: everything, glob include and exclude patterns, explicit paths, GGUF quants, or for datasets Configs, Splits and Parquet-only.

  1. Plan. Hangar resolves the Revision, fetches the upstream git history so Commits, trees and pointer files match exactly, lists the files with their sizes and SHA-256 values and applies the selection. Objects already anywhere in the Instance are marked present without a transfer. The Mirror's branches point at the upstream Commits as soon as planning finishes, so you can browse the history straight away.
  2. Transfer. One pull.file Job per missing object streams it from the Upstream into the Blob store, hashing as it goes. Interrupted transfers resume with HTTP ranges, and an object that does not match its SHA-256 or size is rejected and retried, so nothing unverified becomes visible.
  3. Finish. Hangar indexes and scans the new Commit, resolves Dependencies and fires the pull.completed webhook. If some files still failed after their retries, the Pull ends partial, with an error per file and a Retry failed action.

Small, non-LFS files come with the git history and need no transfer.

docs.title: Network controls
docs.text: Admins can cap the bandwidth Pulls use across the whole Instance, limit how many files transfer at once, and confine Pulls to time windows such as 01:00-07:00. See Pull windows and bandwidth.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
After indexing a Commit, Hangar reads the files that name other Repos:

Source Finds Kind Pulled automatically auto_map in config.json, tokenizer_config.json and the other config files Remote code in another Repo, as in jinaai/xlm-roberta-flash-implementation--modeling_lora.XLMRobertaLoRA code Yes, recursively (pull.dependencies.auto_pull_code) adapter_config.json base_model_name_or_path A PEFT adapter's base model adapter_base Only with pull.dependencies.auto_pull_base_models Model card base_model Where the model came from card_base_model No Model card datasets Training datasets dataset No modules.json, model_index.json sentence-transformers and diffusers components in other Repos code Yes

A Pull is not complete until its code Dependencies are, so from_pretrained(..., trust_remote_code=True) works offline right after it. Suggested Dependencies are listed on the Repo page and by hangar info, each with a one-click Pull.

docs.title: Repos and Revisions
docs.text:
A Repo is a real git repository with a type, model or dataset, and an ID of the form namespace/name, such as acme/sentiment-small or, for a dataset, datasets/acme/reviews in URLs. A model and a dataset can share the same namespace/name.

The Hub HTTP API, git and the web UI are three views of the same Commits: a file uploaded with huggingface_hub appears in git log, and a git push shows up in model_info.

docs.title: Revisions
docs.text:
A Revision names a Commit: a branch (main), a tag (v1.0), a full Commit SHA, or a pull request ref (refs/pr/1). Commit SHAs are git SHA-1 values, as on huggingface.co, and a Mirror keeps the upstream SHAs, so a Revision pinned in code resolves to the same files.

Datasets also have refs/convert/parquet, the branch that holds their Parquet export.

docs.title: Large files
docs.text:
Files that .gitattributes tracks with LFS (weights, archives, Parquet and so on) are stored whole in the Blob store and addressed by SHA-256. git trees hold a small pointer instead. An object that already exists anywhere in the Instance is never stored twice, so two Repos with the same weights use the space once.

Hangar never chunks or transforms your files: an admin can recover any file from the Blob store with standard tools, at lfs/sha256/<first 2>/<next 2>/<sha256>.

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text: Visibility Who can read public Anyone signed in, and anonymous users if the Instance allows anonymous reads (security.anonymous_read). internal Any signed-in user. private Members of the Namespace and the Repo's collaborators.

docs.title: Renames, transfers and deletes
docs.text: Renaming a Repo or moving it to another Namespace keeps redirects from the old ID, for the HTTP API, git and the UI. Deleting a Repo is a soft delete: an admin can restore it for repos.restore_window (7 days by default), after which it is purged.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
Pick the way you want to run Hangar. Each takes a few minutes on a clean machine. System requirements says what each needs, and how much disk to plan for.

Option Best for Docker Trying Hangar, a laptop or a single homelab server. Docker Compose Postgres and S3 storage, a scaled-out setup, or trying OIDC sign-in. Helm Kubernetes. Binary Running without containers, or the hangar CLI on your own machine.

Then:

  1. Sign in for the first time and create a Token.
  2. Pull your first model into the Arsenal.
  3. Point HF_ENDPOINT at Hangar, so your Python code uses it.

docs.title: Run the hangar binary
docs.text:
One binary is both the server and the client. Install it with any of these:

Release archiveHomebrewgo install

Download the archive for your system from the releases page, check it, and put hangar on your PATH. Set VERSION to the release you want, without the v:

VERSION=1.2.3
curl -LO "https://github.com/hangar-hub/hangar/releases/download/v$VERSION/checksums.txt"
curl -LO "https://github.com/hangar-hub/hangar/releases/download/v$VERSION/hangar_${VERSION}_linux_amd64.tar.gz"
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c checksums.txt
tar xzf "hangar_${VERSION}_linux_amd64.tar.gz" hangar && sudo mv hangar /usr/local/bin/
hangar version

On macOS, download hangar_${VERSION}_darwin_arm64.tar.gz (or darwin_amd64 on an Intel Mac) and check it with shasum -a 256 --ignore-missing -c checksums.txt. To check that checksums.txt itself came from Hangar's release workflow, verify its signature as Verify the image describes.

Archives are built for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64, named hangar_<version>_<os>_<arch>: .tar.gz for Linux and macOS, and .zip for Windows. CI tests the server on Linux only; see Tested versions and platforms.

Each archive also has shell completion scripts in its completions folder. To turn them on, see Turn on tab completion.

brew install --cask hangar-hub/tap/hangar

The cask removes macOS's quarantine attribute from the binary when it installs it, because the binary is not notarised, so Gatekeeper does not check it. brew upgrade --cask hangar-hub/tap/hangar installs new releases. The cask also installs tab completion for bash, zsh and fish.

go install github.com/hangar-hub/hangar/cmd/hangar@latest

This builds without the web UI embedded, which is fine for the CLI, and hangar version reports dev. Use a release archive or the image to run a server with the UI.

docs.title: Run a server
docs.text:
The server needs git 2.39 or later on the PATH.

hangar server --public-url http://localhost:8080 \
  --set server.data_dir="$HOME/hangar" \
  --set database.dsn="$HOME/hangar/hangar.db" \
  --set storage.fs.path="$HOME/hangar/blobs" \
  --set git.cache_dir="$HOME/.cache/hangar/git"

The first start generates an admin password and an Instance key and saves them in secrets.yaml in server.data_dir, here $HOME/hangar/secrets.yaml. It prints the admin password only when you run it in a terminal; otherwise read it with grep bootstrap_admin_password "$HOME/hangar/secrets.yaml". It never prints the Instance key. Keys can also come from a YAML file (--config hangar.yaml) or HANGAR_* environment variables; see the configuration reference.

docs.title: Use the CLI
docs.text:
hangar login --url http://localhost:8080
hangar pull hf-internal-testing/tiny-random-bert

See The hangar CLI.

docs.title: Run Hangar with Docker Compose
docs.text:
The repository has four Compose examples in deploy/compose. CI starts each of them and runs the smoke test against it.

File What it runs quickstart.yaml One Hangar container with SQLite and the filesystem Blob store. postgres-minio.yaml Hangar with Postgres and MinIO, the setup to grow from. The bucket is created on start. scale.yaml Two web replicas behind Traefik, two worker replicas, Postgres, MinIO and an OpenTelemetry Collector that prints what it receives. oidc-keycloak.yaml Hangar with Keycloak and an imported realm, for trying OIDC sign-in.

Get the files:

git clone https://github.com/hangar-hub/hangar.git
cd hangar/deploy/compose

docs.title: Create the secrets
docs.text:
The examples have no default passwords: every secret comes from a variable, and Compose stops with an error that names the variable if it is missing. Create them once, in a .env file next to the Compose files, which Docker Compose reads for every example in the folder:

(umask 077 && set -C && cat > .env) <<EOF
HANGAR_INSTANCE_KEY=$(openssl rand -base64 32)
HANGAR_ADMIN_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -base64 18)
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 24)
MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 24)
KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 24)
HANGAR_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 24)
EOF

umask 077 makes the file readable by you only, and set -C stops the command from overwriting a .env you already have: Postgres and MinIO keep the passwords they started with, so changing them later locks Hangar out of its own data. The .env file is in .gitignore. Keep a copy of HANGAR_INSTANCE_KEY, which encrypts stored secrets.

Variable Used by HANGAR_ADMIN_PASSWORD Every example: the password of the first admin, hangar-admin. quickstart.yaml, postgres-minio.yaml and oidc-keycloak.yaml generate one into secrets.yaml in their data volume if it is not set; scale.yaml needs it. HANGAR_INSTANCE_KEY scale.yaml, where every replica needs the same key. The other examples generate one into their data volume. POSTGRES_PASSWORD, MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD postgres-minio.yaml and scale.yaml. KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD, HANGAR_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET oidc-keycloak.yaml.

Docker Compose reads these names, not Hangar: the examples pass each value to Hangar under its own configuration variable, such as HANGAR_SECURITY_INSTANCE_KEY for HANGAR_INSTANCE_KEY. Do not load .env into a shell that runs hangar commands, or pass these names to docker run -e: Hangar refuses to start when it sees a HANGAR_ variable that is not one of its configuration keys. See Troubleshooting.

Only Hangar's port is published on every network interface. The MinIO console, the Traefik dashboard and Keycloak are published on 127.0.0.1, so you can open them on this machine and nobody else on your network can. Postgres and the MinIO API are not published at all.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
docker compose -f quickstart.yaml up -d
# The generated admin password, if .env does not set one:
docker compose -f quickstart.yaml cp hangar:/var/lib/hangar/secrets.yaml - | tar -xO | grep bootstrap_admin_password

docs.title: Postgres and MinIO
docs.text:
docker compose -f postgres-minio.yaml up -d

Sign in as hangar-admin with HANGAR_ADMIN_PASSWORD. The MinIO console is at http://127.0.0.1:9001 (user hangar, password MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD). MinIO's root user can read and change every LFS object and all git data without going through Hangar's permissions, so do not publish the console on other interfaces.

Downloads and uploads go through Hangar in this example (storage.s3.download_mode: proxy and storage.s3.upload_mode: proxy), because your browser and your clients cannot reach http://minio:9000. If MinIO has a public address, set HANGAR_STORAGE_S3_ENDPOINT to it and remove HANGAR_STORAGE_S3_DOWNLOAD_MODE and HANGAR_STORAGE_S3_UPLOAD_MODE, so clients download from and upload to MinIO directly.

docs.title: Scaled out
docs.text:
docker compose -f scale.yaml up -d
docker compose -f scale.yaml logs -f otel-collector

Every replica reads the same HANGAR_INSTANCE_KEY and HANGAR_ADMIN_PASSWORD from .env. A one-off migrate service applies database migrations before the web and worker replicas start. Hangar is at http://localhost:8080 and the Traefik dashboard at http://127.0.0.1:8082. See Scaling.

docs.title: OIDC with Keycloak
docs.text:
docker compose -f oidc-keycloak.yaml up -d

Open http://localhost:8080 and choose Sign in with Keycloak. The realm has two users: alice (password alice-password, an Instance admin through the hangar-admins group) and bob (password bob-password, a write Member of the ml Organisation through the ml-team group). Keycloak answers at http://keycloak.localhost:8081; browsers resolve any *.localhost name to your machine, and the Hangar container reaches Keycloak at the same address through a network alias, so the issuer matches on both sides. Keycloak is published on 127.0.0.1 only, so these example users and its admin console (user admin, password KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD) are reachable from this machine only. The realm reads the hangar client's secret from HANGAR_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET and its redirect URI from HANGAR_PUBLIC_URL, so sign-in works on another port too. See OIDC with Keycloak.

docs.title: Use another image
docs.text:
Every example takes HANGAR_IMAGE, HANGAR_PORT and HANGAR_PUBLIC_URL. HANGAR_PUBLIC_URL defaults to http://localhost: followed by HANGAR_PORT; set it when people reach Hangar at another address.

HANGAR_IMAGE=ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:1.2.3 HANGAR_PORT=9090 \
  docker compose -f quickstart.yaml up -d

The examples run ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:latest by default. On an Instance other people rely on, pin a version instead: 1.2.3 for one release, or 1.2 to get patch releases of 1.2 only. Put HANGAR_IMAGE in .env to keep the pin, and change it when you upgrade. The releases page lists every version.

docs.title: Run Hangar with Docker
docs.text:
One container, with SQLite and the filesystem Blob store in a volume.

docker run -d --name hangar -p 8080:8080 -v hangar:/var/lib/hangar \
  -e HANGAR_SERVER_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:8080 \
  ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:latest

HANGAR_SERVER_PUBLIC_URL is the URL clients use to reach Hangar. It appears in git URLs, LFS links and redirects, so set it to the address your users type, such as https://hangar.example.com behind a reverse proxy.

On the first start Hangar generates an Instance key and a password for the first admin and saves them in /var/lib/hangar/secrets.yaml (mode 0600). The container log names the file but never holds the secrets, because log collectors can read it. The image has no shell, so copy the password out of the volume with docker cp:

docker cp hangar:/var/lib/hangar/secrets.yaml - | tar -xO | grep bootstrap_admin_password

bootstrap_admin_password: XLhYPMrxhrVxjJDFmpPcPtVy

The file also holds instance_key. Keep a copy of it: it encrypts stored secrets such as upstream tokens and webhook secrets. Later starts read both from the file.

docs.title: The image
docs.text:
• ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:<version> and :latest, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, signed with cosign (see Security hardening).
  • It runs as UID 65532 with no shell, and works with a read-only root filesystem when /tmp and /var/cache/hangar are writable:
docker run -d --name hangar -p 8080:8080 -v hangar:/var/lib/hangar \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /var/cache/hangar:uid=65532,gid=65532 \
  -e HANGAR_SERVER_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:8080 \
  ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:latest
  • Data lives in /var/lib/hangar, the git pack cache in /var/cache/hangar.
  • The image has a HEALTHCHECK that runs hangar healthcheck, which calls /readyz.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Every configuration key is also an environment variable: storage.s3.bucket is HANGAR_STORAGE_S3_BUCKET. To use a file instead, mount it at /etc/hangar/hangar.yaml, where the image reads it (the image sets HANGAR_CONFIG to that path). Environment variables override the file.

docker run -d --name hangar -p 8080:8080 -v hangar:/var/lib/hangar \
  -v "$PWD/hangar.yaml:/etc/hangar/hangar.yaml:ro" \
  ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:latest

Every key is listed in the configuration reference. Hangar refuses to start if a HANGAR_ variable is not one of them, so a misspelt name shows up at once; see Troubleshooting.

Next: First sign-in.

docs.title: Sign in for the first time
docs.text:
1. Open Hangar's public URL, such as http://localhost:8080.
  2. Sign in as hangar-admin with the password Hangar generated on first start, or the one you set in HANGAR_SECURITY_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD. Hangar saves a generated password as bootstrap_admin_password in secrets.yaml in server.data_dir; with Docker, read it with docker cp hangar:/var/lib/hangar/secrets.yaml - | tar -xO | grep bootstrap_admin_password.
  3. Choose your own password: open Settings, Profile, enter the generated password as the current password, then your new password twice, and select Change password. The new password needs at least 10 characters and cannot be a common password. Your other sessions are signed out; this one stays signed in. On the same page you can set your display name and email.

docs.title: Create a Token
docs.text:
Clients send a Token as a bearer token (Hub API and native API) or as the git password. Only git and git-lfs accept a Token as a password.

  1. Open Settings, Tokens, and select Create Token.
  2. Choose a scope: read to download, write to also upload and start Pulls, or admin for every other kind of administration. Permissions lists what each scope allows. You can limit a Token to some Namespaces or Repos, and give it an expiry.
  3. Copy the secret, which starts with hgr_. It is shown once.

Or let the CLI create one with a device-code sign-in:

hangar login --url http://localhost:8080

docs.title: Add people
docs.text:
Self-registration is off by default (security.registration: closed). As an admin, open Admin, Users to create invite links, or connect an OIDC provider so people sign in with accounts they already have; see OIDC.

Next: Pull your first model.

docs.title: Pull your first model
docs.text: A Pull fetches a Repo, or some of its files, from an Upstream such as huggingface.co into the Arsenal. It keeps the upstream ID and Commit SHAs, so code that names org/model works against Hangar unchanged.

docs.title: From the web UI
docs.text:
1. Open Discover and search by name, or enter a full Repo ID such as hf-internal-testing/tiny-random-bert.
  2. Open a result, or for a Repo ID select Open hf-internal-testing/tiny-random-bert. The huggingface.co search does not list every Repo (it leaves out hf-internal-testing, for example), so a Repo ID opens the Repo directly. Hangar shows the files, their sizes, any GGUF quants and the Dependencies it would pull.
  3. Select Pull into arsenal. The Pull runs as a Job; follow it under Jobs.

For a GGUF Repo, the quant picker lets you pull one quantisation, such as Q4_K_M, instead of every file. The Repo then becomes a Partial mirror: the full history is there, and files you did not pull show as Not in arsenal with a Pull action.

docs.title: From the CLI
docs.text:
hangar pull hf-internal-testing/tiny-random-bert
hangar pull bartowski/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-GGUF:Q4_K_M

hangar pull asks the Instance to pull what is missing, shows the progress, then downloads the files into your local Hugging Face cache, where Python libraries find them. Add --server-only to fill the Arsenal without downloading to your machine.

docs.title: Gated and private Repos
docs.text:
Pulls of gated or private Repos need your huggingface.co token. Save it under Settings, Upstream tokens; Pulls you start use it. See Gated models.

Next: Point HF_ENDPOINT at Hangar.

docs.title: Run Hangar on Kubernetes with Helm
docs.text: The chart is published as an OCI artefact at oci://ghcr.io/hangar-hub/charts/hangar.

docs.title: One Pod with SQLite
docs.text:
The default runs one Pod in role all, with SQLite and the filesystem Blob store on a PersistentVolumeClaim:

helm install hangar oci://ghcr.io/hangar-hub/charts/hangar \
  --namespace hangar --create-namespace \
  --set publicURL=https://hangar.example.com \
  --set ingress.enabled=true --set ingress.className=nginx \
  --set 'ingress.hosts[0].host=hangar.example.com'

The chart generates the Instance key and the first admin password into a Secret named after the release with -generated added, hangar-generated for the release hangar, and keeps them across upgrades by reading the Secret back from the cluster. (A release whose name does not contain hangar, such as models, gets models-hangar-generated.) Read the password:

kubectl get secret --namespace hangar hangar-generated \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.HANGAR_SECURITY_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d; echo

With persistence on, the chart refuses to render more than one replica or any workers, because SQLite and a ReadWriteOnce volume belong to one Pod.

Generated secrets need helm install or helm upgrade with access to the cluster. helm template, helm lint, --dry-run=client and Argo CD cannot read the cluster, so they would make a new Instance key on every render, and Hangar could no longer decrypt the upstream tokens and webhook secrets it stored with the old one. The chart stops with an error there instead. Set existingSecret for those tools, as described in Run with Argo CD.

docs.title: Scaled out with Postgres and S3
docs.text:
Turn persistence off, point the configuration at Postgres and a bucket, and choose replicas:

# values.yaml
publicURL: https://hangar.example.com
persistence:
  enabled: false
config:
  database: {driver: postgres}
  storage:
    backend: s3
    s3: {endpoint: s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com, region: eu-west-2, bucket: my-hangar}
existingSecret: hangar-secrets   # HANGAR_DATABASE_DSN, HANGAR_SECURITY_INSTANCE_KEY, ...
web:
  replicas: 2
  autoscaling: {enabled: true, minReplicas: 2, maxReplicas: 6}
  podDisruptionBudget: {enabled: true}
worker:
  replicas: 2
serviceAccount:
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/hangar   # IRSA for S3

kubectl create secret generic hangar-secrets --namespace hangar \
  --from-literal=HANGAR_DATABASE_DSN='postgres://hangar:...@postgres:5432/hangar' \
  --from-literal=HANGAR_SECURITY_INSTANCE_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
  --from-literal=HANGAR_SECURITY_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD="$(openssl rand -base64 18)"
helm install hangar oci://ghcr.io/hangar-hub/charts/hangar --namespace hangar -f values.yaml

Every web and worker Pod must have the same Instance key, and Hangar refuses to start in those roles without one. Give it through existingSecret as above, through secrets, or let the chart generate it (generateSecrets, the default, which needs helm install or helm upgrade). A render that gives the Pods no key stops with an error.

A pre-install and pre-upgrade Job runs hangar admin migrate, and web and worker Pods report ready only when the schema is at the version they expect. With migrations.mode: initContainer, each web and worker Pod runs the migration in an init container instead, with no Helm hooks; see Run with Argo CD. A fuller example is deploy/helm/examples/scale-values.yaml.

docs.title: Run with Argo CD
docs.text:
Argo CD, Flux and other GitOps tools render the chart with helm template and apply the result. Two things differ from helm install:

  • Hooks run first. Argo CD runs Helm's pre-install and pre-upgrade hooks as PreSync hooks, before anything else in the Application. If Postgres is in the same Application, the migrate Job waits for a database that Argo CD has not created yet, and the first sync never finishes. Set migrations.mode: initContainer: every web and worker Pod then runs hangar admin migrate in an init container, which waits for the database to answer for up to migrations.waitForDatabase (5 minutes by default), then fails, and the kubelet restarts it. Migrations hold a lock in the database, so when several Pods start together, one migrates and the others wait for it instead of failing. Postgres releases the lock when the migrating Pod's connection ends, so a Pod killed mid-migration does not block the next one.
  • No cluster access while rendering. lookup returns nothing, so the chart cannot keep generated secrets and stops with an error if generateSecrets would generate them. Create the Secret yourself and name it in existingSecret.
  • The test Pod is a hook too. The chart's helm test Pod carries helm.sh/hook: test. Argo CD skips it, but helm template renders it as an ordinary Pod. A tool that applies the render as it is, such as kubectl apply or Kustomize's helmCharts, starts it before Hangar is up, and it stays in Error. Pass --skip-tests to helm template, or set skipTests: true in Kustomize's helmCharts entry.

Create the namespace and the Secret once, outside your git repository or with a secrets operator such as Sealed Secrets or External Secrets:

kubectl create namespace hangar
kubectl create secret generic hangar-secrets --namespace hangar \
  --from-literal=HANGAR_DATABASE_DSN='postgres://hangar:<password>@postgres:5432/hangar' \
  --from-literal=HANGAR_STORAGE_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID='<access key ID>' \
  --from-literal=HANGAR_STORAGE_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY='<secret access key>' \
  --from-literal=HANGAR_SECURITY_INSTANCE_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
  --from-literal=HANGAR_SECURITY_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD="$(openssl rand -base64 18)"

Back up HANGAR_SECURITY_INSTANCE_KEY: without it, stored upstream tokens and webhook secrets cannot be decrypted.

Then point an Application at the chart with values like deploy/helm/examples/gitops-values.yaml:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: hangar
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: hangar
  source:
    repoURL: ghcr.io/hangar-hub/charts
    chart: hangar
    targetRevision: 1.2.3   # the chart version to deploy, which is also the Hangar version
    helm:
      releaseName: hangar
      valuesObject:
        publicURL: https://hangar.example.com
        persistence: {enabled: false}
        config:
          database: {driver: postgres}
          storage:
            backend: s3
            # region: the region your MinIO is configured with.
            s3: {endpoint: minio.example.com, region: us-east-1, bucket: hangar, use_path_style: true}
        existingSecret: hangar-secrets
        generateSecrets: false
        migrations: {mode: initContainer}
        web: {replicas: 1}
        worker: {replicas: 1}
  syncPolicy:
    automated: {prune: true, selfHeal: true}

Argo CD pulls OCI charts from a Helm repository with enableOCI: true; add ghcr.io/hangar-hub/charts as one, as the Argo CD Helm guide describes. Set releaseName: hangar so resource names match the rest of this guide. Argo CD skips the chart's helm test Pod, and the PersistentVolumeClaim and generated Secret keep helm.sh/resource-policy: keep, which Argo CD treats as Delete=false.
