If no answer comes in that time, it prints one line to say so and asks again: the Instance carries on checking in the meantime, so nothing is uploaded twice.

Symbolic links are followed only to files inside the folder, or to files in a Hugging Face cache, such as the files of a cache snapshot or the files hangar lmstudio links into LM Studio's folder. hangar push skips any other link and names it, so a folder you did not make yourself cannot send a file from elsewhere on your machine. Copy such a file into the folder to upload it.

docs.title: Your own models, not on any Upstream
docs.text: Repos you upload are ordinary Repos: they have the same history, browsing, indexing and security scanning as Mirrors, and you can share them through Organisations, collaborators or visibility. Models you already have on disk, in a Hugging Face cache, LM Studio or Ollama, can be imported without downloading them again.

docs.title: Use vLLM
docs.text:
vLLM downloads models with huggingface_hub, so HF_ENDPOINT points it at Hangar. Every vLLM server then loads weights from your own network instead of huggingface.co, and a model pinned to a Commit SHA loads the same files it would there.

Hangar's CI tests the huggingface_hub downloads that vLLM uses, but does not run vLLM itself; see Tested versions and platforms.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
1. Pull the model into the Arsenal. --server-only fills the Arsenal without downloading the files to your machine:

    hangar pull Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --server-only

    vLLM reads the config, tokenizer and generation config files as well as the weights, so pull the whole Repo, not only the weights. If you pull only some files, the Repo becomes a Partial mirror and vLLM fails on the first file that is not present. An admin can instead turn on Pull-through, so a request for a missing Repo or file pulls it.

  2. Create a read Token for the servers under Settings, Tokens. A Token can be limited to the Repos it serves.

docs.title: Serve a model
docs.text:
export HF_ENDPOINT=https://hangar.example.com
export HF_TOKEN=hgr_...
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B

Mirrors keep the upstream Commit SHAs, so a Revision pinned for huggingface.co works unchanged:

vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --revision <commit SHA>

docs.title: In a container
docs.text:
docker run --gpus all -p 8000:8000 \
  -e HF_ENDPOINT=https://hangar.example.com -e HF_TOKEN=hgr_... \
  -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  vllm/vllm-openai:latest --model Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B

Mounting the cache means a restart loads from disk without asking Hangar again.

docs.title: On Kubernetes
docs.text: Keep the Token in a Secret and the Hugging Face cache on a volume, so a restarted Pod does not download the model again. Load models in Kubernetes without downloading them on every Pod start has a complete Deployment for vLLM, with an init container that downloads the model from Hangar before the server starts.

docs.title: Start with no network
docs.text:
For a fully offline start, download the files once into the local cache, then set HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1:

hangar pull Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B

hangar pull writes into the same Hugging Face cache vLLM reads.

docs.title: Errors you may see
docs.text:
Error Cause Fix RepositoryNotFoundError, "Repository Not Found for url" HF_TOKEN is missing or cannot read the Repo, or the Repo is not in the Arsenal. Private Repos answer as if they did not exist. Check the Token with HF_TOKEN=hgr_... hf auth whoami, and pull the Repo first. "Invalid credentials in Authorization header" The Token is wrong, expired or revoked, or it is a huggingface.co token (hf_...) rather than a Hangar one (hgr_...). Create a Token in Hangar. RemoteEntryNotFoundError with status 409, saying the file is not in the arsenal The Repo is a Partial mirror and the file was not pulled. Run the hangar pull command it names, or pull the whole Repo. LocalEntryNotFoundError with HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 The files are not in the local cache. Run hangar pull for the model, or start once without HF_HUB_OFFLINE.

For other problems, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
Webhooks send an HTTP POST to your URL when something happens in a Namespace or Repo: pushes and Commits, Pulls, Mirror syncs, indexing and scans, discussions and pull requests. The event list and payloads are in Webhook events.

Create one under the Namespace's or Repo's Settings, Webhooks, with the URL, a secret and the events you want. Admins of the Namespace or Repo can manage them, see each delivery with its status code and duration, redeliver it, and send a test event.

docs.title: Verify the signature
docs.text:
Every delivery carries X-Hangar-Signature: sha256=<hex>, an HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body with your secret. Check it before you trust the payload:

import hashlib, hmac

def verify(secret: bytes, body: bytes, header: str) -> bool:
    expected = "sha256=" + hmac.new(secret, body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)

X-Hangar-Event names the event and X-Hangar-Delivery identifies the delivery, so you can ignore repeats.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text: A delivery that does not answer 2xx within 10 seconds is retried after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours and 12 hours, then marked failed.

docs.title: Private addresses
docs.text:
By default, webhooks cannot target private addresses: loopback, RFC 1918, carrier-grade NAT and unique local addresses. A delivery to one fails with "webhook targets a private address, which this Instance does not allow". To deliver to a service on your LAN, an Instance admin turns on Allow webhooks to private addresses under Admin, Settings, or sets webhooks.allow_private_targets: true in the configuration. Only do this when everyone who can add a webhook may reach your internal network through Hangar: every user administers their own Namespace, so every user can add one.

Earlier releases allowed private targets by default. If your webhooks deliver to private addresses, an admin must now turn the setting on.

Whatever the setting, Hangar never delivers to link-local addresses (which include the cloud metadata service at 169.254.169.254), other cloud metadata addresses, 0.0.0.0 or multicast addresses. Hangar checks the address it connects to after resolving the host name, and does not follow redirects.

docs.title: Operate
docs.text:
Running Hangar for yourself or for many people.

  • Configuration: every key, its environment variable and default.
  • Storage backends and databases.
  • Scaling: process roles, replicas and what is shared.
  • OIDC: sign-in through your identity provider.
  • TLS and reverse proxies.
  • Observability: traces, metrics, logs and dashboards.
  • Backup and restore, upgrades, security hardening and troubleshooting.
  • Uninstall, and where Hangar keeps data.

docs.title: Back up and restore
docs.text:
What to back up:

  • The database (SQLite file or Postgres).
  • The Blob store (the storage.fs.path folder, or the bucket).
  • The Instance key (security.instance_key, or secrets.yaml in server.data_dir). Without it, saved upstream tokens and webhook secrets cannot be decrypted.

docs.title: hangar admin backup
docs.text:
hangar admin backup reads the configuration like hangar server does and writes a folder with:

  • manifest.json: the Hangar version, schema version, database driver, row counts and object counts;
  • db/<table>.jsonl: every table, read in one transaction, so it is consistent, except the Repo listing facts (repo_facts, repo_facet_values and repo_facts_changes), which Hangar rebuilds from the other tables after a restore;
  • blobs/<key>: every Blob store object, except staging areas.
hangar admin backup --config /etc/hangar/hangar.yaml --output /backups/hangar-$(date +%F)

Objects are copied after the database. They never change once written, and garbage collection keeps unreferenced objects for gc.grace_period (7 days), so every object the database refers to is in the backup.

hangar admin restore loads a backup into an empty database, migrated to the same schema version, in one transaction, and copies objects that the Blob store does not already have:

hangar admin restore /backups/hangar-2026-10-13 --config /etc/hangar/hangar.yaml

A backup made on SQLite restores into Postgres and the other way round, and a filesystem backup restores into S3 and the other way round, so restore is also how you move between backends. Restore with the Hangar version that made the backup, then upgrade. --force empties a database that is not empty first.

Stop Hangar before you restore. Keep a copy of the Instance key: a restore needs it, but store it separately from the backup.

docs.title: Per backend combination
docs.text:
Setup Back up with Notes SQLite and filesystem (one container) hangar admin backup with Hangar stopped, or a snapshot of the volume with Hangar stopped SQLite allows one process, so admin backup cannot run beside the server. With Docker, see Back up a container. Postgres and filesystem hangar admin backup while running, or pg_dump plus a filesystem snapshot or rsync of the storage.fs.path folder Take the database dump before the files. Postgres and S3 hangar admin backup --skip-blobs (or pg_dump) plus bucket versioning or replication Copying a large bucket through Hangar is slow; S3's own replication is better. Take the database backup first. SQLite and S3 hangar admin backup --skip-blobs with Hangar stopped, plus bucket versioning or replication

Test your restores: restore into a scratch Instance and run hangar admin doctor against it.

docs.title: Back up a container
docs.text:
The image runs Hangar as UID 65532 and has a /backups folder that belongs to that user. Mount a named volume there: a new named volume takes the owner of the folder it is mounted on, so Hangar can write to it.

docker stop hangar
docker run --rm -v hangar:/var/lib/hangar -v hangar-backups:/backups \
  ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:latest admin backup --output /backups/$(date +%F)
docker start hangar

To copy a backup out of the volume, create a container that mounts it and use docker cp:

docker create --name hangar-backup-copy -v hangar-backups:/backups ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:latest
docker cp hangar-backup-copy:/backups/2026-10-14 ./hangar-backup-2026-10-14
docker rm hangar-backup-copy

To restore, mount the same volume. Restoring into the Instance's own volume keeps the Instance key in secrets.yaml, and --force empties the database first:

docker stop hangar
docker run --rm -v hangar:/var/lib/hangar -v hangar-backups:/backups:ro \
  ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:latest admin restore /backups/2026-10-14 --force
docker start hangar

To write the backup to a folder on a Linux host instead, give the folder to UID 65532 first. A folder that belongs to root, as a new one usually does, fails with permission denied. Running the container with --user does not help, because then Hangar cannot read its own data volume.

sudo install -d -o 65532 -g 65532 -m 0700 /srv/hangar-backups
docker run --rm -v hangar:/var/lib/hangar -v /srv/hangar-backups:/backups \
  ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:latest admin backup --output /backups/$(date +%F)

The backup files belong to UID 65532 with mode 0600, so read them on the host with sudo.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text: Hangar keeps metadata, refs, Jobs and sessions in SQLite or Postgres. The schema is the same on both.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
database:
  driver: sqlite
  dsn: /var/lib/hangar/hangar.db

SQLite is for one process in role all: Hangar holds a lock file next to the database and refuses to start a second process against it. Keep the database on a local disk, not a network share.

docs.title: Postgres
docs.text:
database:
  driver: postgres
  dsn: postgres://hangar:password@postgres:5432/hangar?sslmode=require
  max_open_conns: 20

Postgres supports any number of web and worker processes. Hangar is tested with Postgres 18. Put the DSN in a secret (HANGAR_DATABASE_DSN), not in a configuration file.

database.driver defaults to sqlite, so set it to postgres (HANGAR_DATABASE_DRIVER=postgres) as well as the DSN. With the sqlite driver, Hangar refuses a DSN that is a URL other than file: and names the setting to change.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
Processes in role all apply migrations when they start. With separate web and worker processes, run migrations once before starting them:

hangar admin migrate

The Helm chart and the scaled Compose example do this for you. web and worker processes report not ready on /readyz until the schema is at the version they expect.

docs.title: Moving from SQLite to Postgres
docs.text: Back up with SQLite configured, then restore with Postgres configured; see Backup and restore.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Hangar exports traces, metrics and logs with OpenTelemetry, over OTLP, and needs no vendor agent. With nothing configured it makes no connections and writes JSON logs to standard output.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
The standard OpenTelemetry variables work and win over Hangar's own settings:

OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://otlp.example.com:4318
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf          # or grpc
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=Bearer ..."
OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=deployment.environment.name=production

Or in configuration: telemetry.traces, telemetry.metrics and telemetry.logs (otlp, console or none; metrics also prometheus), telemetry.service_name, telemetry.environment, telemetry.log_format and telemetry.log_level. With telemetry.metrics: prometheus, Hangar serves /metrics on telemetry.prometheus_listen (:9464 by default).

What Hangar sends:

  • Traces: one span per request, named after the route template (such as GET /{ns}/{name}/resolve/{rev}/{path}), with child spans for database queries, Blob store operations, Upstream requests, git work and Jobs. Spans carry hangar.protocol, hangar.repo.id and the user ID when signed in.
  • Metrics: HTTP server metrics by hangar.protocol, Go runtime metrics, and Hangar's own, listed in the metrics reference.
  • Logs: every log line, with trace_id and span_id inside a request or Job and request_id inside a request; one access log line per request; and audit events as hangar.audit.<action> records.

Hangar never records tokens, passwords, cookies, presigned URLs or Authorization headers on spans or logs. Repo IDs are on spans and logs, never metric attributes.

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
• /healthz answers 200 while the process is alive.
  • /readyz answers 200 when the database is reachable, migrations are at the expected version, the Blob store answers and the server has finished starting, and 503 with the failed checks otherwise. Load balancers and Kubernetes should use it. The Blob store check runs in the background with its own 5-second timeout and its result is reused for 10 seconds, so a probe that gives up early does not make the next probes fail. Each check may take up to 5 seconds and /readyz answers within 10 seconds in all; a check left no time is reported as not run. Probes should wait longer than 10 seconds: the Helm chart waits 15.

docs.title: Elastic
docs.text:
Send OTLP to an EDOT Collector, the Elastic managed OTLP endpoint, or an Elastic Observability project:

OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://<project>.ingest.<region>.elastic.cloud:443
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=ApiKey <key>"

Traces appear in APM as the hangar service. Import the Kibana dashboard: Stack Management, Saved objects, Import, and choose deploy/dashboards/kibana/hangar.ndjson. It needs Kibana 9.4 or later and reads the logs-*.otel-* and metrics-*.otel-* data streams. Keep the default cumulative temporality for metrics; the dashboard computes rates from cumulative counters.

docs.title: Grafana stack
docs.text:
Send OTLP to Grafana Alloy or an OpenTelemetry Collector that writes to Tempo, Prometheus or Mimir, and Loki; or scrape Hangar's Prometheus endpoint directly. Import deploy/dashboards/grafana/hangar.json under Dashboards, New, Import, and choose your Prometheus data source.

The dashboard uses the names the Prometheus exporter gives (hangar_download_bytes_total, http_server_request_duration_seconds and so on), which are also what Prometheus's own OTLP receiver produces with its default name translation.

docs.title: Any OTLP backend
docs.text: Point OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT at it. The scaled Compose example runs an OpenTelemetry Collector that prints everything it receives, which is a quick way to see the data.

docs.title: TLS and reverse proxies
docs.text:
Hangar serves plain HTTP; put a reverse proxy in front of it for TLS. Whatever proxy you use:

  • Set server.public_url to the address clients use, with https://.
  • Set server.trusted_proxies to the proxy's addresses, so Hangar believes its X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto headers and nobody else's. Without it, every client has the proxy's address: one client's failed sign-ins throttle everyone, and the audit log records the proxy. Hangar logs a warning the first time a request with X-Forwarded-For comes from a peer that is not in the list.
  • Do not buffer request or response bodies, and do not set a total request timeout: uploads and downloads stream and can take hours. Hangar closes connections idle for 5 minutes itself.
  • Allow large request bodies (5 TiB files go up in parts of up to 512 MiB).
  • Route datasets-server.<host> to Hangar as well, for the datasets library (see Datasets).
  • Ollama needs a certificate it trusts, or --insecure.
TraefiknginxCaddyCloudflare Tunnel 
# Docker labels on the Hangar container
traefik.enable: "true"
traefik.http.routers.hangar.rule: Host(`hangar.example.com`) || Host(`datasets-server.hangar.example.com`)
traefik.http.routers.hangar.entrypoints: websecure
traefik.http.routers.hangar.tls.certresolver: letsencrypt
traefik.http.services.hangar.loadbalancer.server.port: "8080"

Traefik streams bodies by default. Set respondingTimeouts.readTimeout and writeTimeout to 0 on the entry point, as the scaled Compose example does.

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name hangar.example.com datasets-server.hangar.example.com;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/hangar.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/hangar.key;

    client_max_body_size 0;
    proxy_request_buffering off;
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_max_temp_file_size 0;
    proxy_read_timeout 1h;
    proxy_send_timeout 1h;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

hangar.example.com, datasets-server.hangar.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080 {
        flush_interval -1
        transport http {
            read_timeout 0
            write_timeout 0
        }
    }
}

Caddy gets and renews certificates itself, and streams request bodies by default.

# cloudflared config.yml
tunnel: <tunnel ID>
credentials-file: /etc/cloudflared/<tunnel ID>.json
ingress:
  - hostname: hangar.example.com
    service: http://hangar:8080
  - hostname: datasets-server.hangar.example.com
    service: http://hangar:8080
  - service: http_status:404

Cloudflare limits request bodies to 100 MB on the Free and Pro plans. Large files still upload, because they go up in parts of 16 MiB or more, each its own request, but a git push sends its pack in one request, so a push with more than 100 MB of non-LFS data fails through the tunnel; push it over your LAN or a direct HTTPS address. Cloudflare Access in front of Hangar also blocks clients that cannot sign in through a browser, such as huggingface_hub, git and Ollama, unless you add service tokens or bypass rules for them.

For Kubernetes, the Helm chart's Ingress and HTTPRoute do the routing; set the controller's body size, buffering and timeout options as above. With the ingress-nginx controller:

# Helm values
ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "0"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-request-buffering: "off"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-max-temp-file-size: "0"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "3600"

docs.title: Large files through nginx
docs.text:
nginx's defaults break large transfers, both in front of Hangar and in front of an S3-compatible store such as MinIO. Every nginx in the path, including Nginx Proxy Manager, needs these settings:

Setting Why proxy_buffering off Streams responses to the client as they arrive, instead of buffering them. proxy_max_temp_file_size 0 Stops nginx spooling a response to disk when the client reads more slowly than the upstream sends. proxy_request_buffering off Streams uploads to the upstream instead of storing the whole body first. client_max_body_size 0 Removes the request size limit (1 MiB by default), which rejects upload parts with 413. proxy_read_timeout 1h, proxy_send_timeout 1h Keeps a slow transfer open; the default of 60 seconds cuts a stalled read or a slow upload part.

With buffering on, nginx writes a response it cannot pass on fast enough to a temporary file, up to proxy_max_temp_file_size, which is 1024 MiB by default. When the file is full, nginx stops reading from the upstream until the client catches up. If the upstream gives up waiting first, it closes the connection, and the client gets a body that ends early. Hangar reads whole objects back from the store when it verifies an upload, so a large file whose read was cut short after about 1 GiB fails with an error such as upload part 65/66: unexpected EOF (64 parts of 16 MiB are 1 GiB), and the client uploads it again. proxy_buffering off and proxy_max_temp_file_size 0 prevent that. Hangar resumes a read that was cut short from where it stopped, so uploads still complete, but each cut costs another request. To check a proxy, run hangar admin doctor --large-read (see Run the doctor).

docs.title: MinIO behind nginx
docs.text:
When clients or Hangar reach MinIO through nginx, for example on https://minio.example.com to get a trusted certificate, give the MinIO server block the same settings:

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name minio.example.com;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/minio.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/minio.key;

    client_max_body_size 0;
    proxy_request_buffering off;
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_max_temp_file_size 0;
    proxy_read_timeout 1h;
    proxy_send_timeout 1h;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:9000;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        # Presigned URLs and request signatures cover the Host header, so
        # pass it through unchanged.
        proxy_set_header Host $http_host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
    }
}

In Nginx Proxy Manager, open the proxy host, select Advanced and add the directives from the table, one per line, ending each with a semicolon. Set storage.s3.endpoint to the nginx address and region to the region MinIO is configured with (see Storage backends).

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
One binary runs in one of three roles (server.role, or hangar server --role):

Role Serves Runs Jobs Scale all (default) Web UI, native API, Hub API, git, Ollama Yes The only role for SQLite. web Everything HTTP No Any number of replicas behind a load balancer. worker Health and metrics only Yes Any number of replicas.

web processes are stateless: everything shared lives in Postgres or the Blob store, so any request can reach any replica, including each request of a git push or a multipart upload. Run them behind a load balancer that does not buffer request or response bodies and has no total request timeout, because uploads and downloads stream.

docs.title: What a scaled-out Instance needs
docs.text:
• Postgres and an S3-compatible bucket (or a shared filesystem path).
  • The same security.instance_key on every process. Hangar generates a key only in role all. A process in role web or worker refuses to start without one, unless it shares a server.data_dir whose secrets.yaml already holds a key. Make a key with openssl rand -base64 32 and give it to every process as HANGAR_SECURITY_INSTANCE_KEY. The Helm chart generates one into a Secret, or reads it from existingSecret.
  • hangar admin migrate before new versions start.
  • Each worker process runs up to jobs.workers Jobs at once (4 by default). pull.concurrency also caps Pull transfers across the Instance.

docs.title: Shutting down
docs.text:
On SIGTERM, a process answers 503 on /readyz at once, and its worker stops claiming new Jobs. It keeps serving for server.drain_delay (0 by default), so a load balancer that checks /readyz stops sending requests before the listener closes. Then in-flight requests get up to server.shutdown_timeout (30 seconds) to finish, and the worker waits as long for its Jobs. A Job whose handler is still running after that goes back to the queue when its lease expires.

Behind a load balancer outside Kubernetes, set server.drain_delay to a little more than the load balancer's health check interval, such as 5s. The Helm chart adds a 5-second preStop sleep (drainDelaySeconds), or sets server.drain_delay on Kubernetes 1.29, which has no sleep action.

The scaled Compose example and the Helm chart show complete setups.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
On the reference setup (two web replicas with 2 vCPU and 1 GiB each, one worker, Postgres and MinIO), Hangar aims for:

Measure Target Repos per Instance 100,000 Files per Repo 100,000 HEAD /resolve p99 at 200 requests per second per replica under 50 ms Memory during a 50 GiB upload or download flat, under 256 MiB per replica Web replica start to ready under 5 seconds

The load tests in loadtest/ measure them.

docs.title: Security hardening
docs.text: This page lists what to do to run Hangar securely. For what Hangar protects, its trust boundaries and the threats it mitigates or leaves to you, see the threat model.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Serve Hangar over HTTPS only, with server.public_url set to the https:// address, and set server.trusted_proxies to your proxy's addresses. Without it, every client shares the proxy's address, so one client's failed sign-ins throttle everyone; Hangar logs a warning when it sees X-Forwarded-For from a peer outside the list.
  • Keep security.registration: closed (the default) or invite, and leave security.anonymous_read off unless you want a public Instance. While it is off, signed-out visitors cannot see public Repos, user and Organisation profiles, member lists or public Collections either.
  • Use OIDC with groups for Instance admins (admin_groups), and turn off local sign-in (security.local_login: false), keeping the bootstrap admin as a break-glass account with a long password stored offline. Failed sign-ins from elsewhere do not lock an account out from addresses it signed in from in the last 90 days; if the bootstrap admin is locked out anyway, clear it with hangar admin unlock-sign-in <username> on the server host.
  • Keep server.public_url on HTTPS so the session and CSRF cookies use the __Host- prefix, and keep security.session_idle_timeout (7 days by default) or shorten it on shared machines.
  • Give Tokens the smallest scope, limit them to the Namespaces or Repos they need, and set an expiry.
  • Tell users to change the password an admin gave them under Settings, Profile. A password change signs out the user's other sessions but keeps their Tokens, so someone who thinks their account was used by someone else should also revoke their Tokens under Settings, Tokens. Wrong current passwords count towards the same throttle as failed sign-ins. Users who forget their password still need a reset link from an admin. When a user changes their email, it waits for confirmation: select Email link next to them under Admin, Users and send the link to the new address, not to the user some other way, because opening it is what proves the address is theirs.
  • Store the Instance key, database DSN and S3 keys in secrets, not configuration files. Rotate the Instance key with hangar admin rotate-key if it leaks.
  • Leave webhooks.allow_private_targets off (the default) on Instances shared with people you do not fully trust, so webhooks cannot reach your internal network. Webhooks and Upstreams never reach link-local or cloud metadata addresses, and a public Upstream cannot redirect Hangar to a private address; see Mirrors and Upstreams.
  • Watch the audit log (Admin, Audit log) and export it with your logs.
  • Run the image as it ships: non-root (UID 65532), read-only root filesystem, no shell. The Helm chart also drops every capability and uses the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile; turn on its NetworkPolicy.
  • Pickle-based weights can run code when loaded. Hangar scans them and shows a warning on suspicious and unsafe files; prefer safetensors. To refuse downloads of risky files, turn on Block downloads of unsafe files under Admin, Settings, and choose whether to block suspicious files too. See Blocking unsafe downloads.

docs.title: Blocking unsafe downloads
docs.text:
With Block downloads of unsafe files on (scan_block_unsafe_downloads in the native API), Hangar refuses to serve:

  • Files the security scan marked unsafe.
  • Files the security scan marked suspicious, when What to block is Unsafe and suspicious files (scan_block_level: suspicious in the native API). The default, Unsafe files (unsafe), lets them download. See Choose what to block.
  • Files that can run code when loaded and that the scan could not read in full, such as a pickle compressed with xz, an old PyTorch tar archive or a joblib file whose array data the scan cannot measure. The scan result shows why.
  • Files that can run code when loaded and have no scan result yet, because the scan is still running or its Job failed. They download once the scan finds them safe. While the scan of a new Commit runs, a file whose content is unchanged since an earlier scanned Commit keeps that Commit's result, in the web UI and for downloads by path.

Files that can run code when loaded are pickle, PyTorch, joblib and NumPy files, by name: .bin, .pt, .pth, .ckpt, .pkl, .pickle, .joblib, .npy and .npz, and those names with a compression or archive suffix (.gz, .bz2, .xz, .lzma, .z, .zst, .lz4, .zip and .tar), such as model.joblib.gz or checkpoint.pth.tar. The scan reads each of them by content, the way torch.load, joblib.load, numpy.load and pandas.read_pickle do: it decompresses compressed files, reads zip archives and .npz members, and follows the NumPy array data that joblib stores inside its pickles. A file that is not a pickle at all, such as OpenVINO weights in a .bin file, is safe. A file that is a pickle but ends part-way gets an error result and still downloads, because every loader stops at the same point.

Hangar scans the Commit at the tip of every branch, tag and pull request. A Commit it has not scanned, such as an earlier Commit of a push, takes the result of the same file in a Commit it has. git-lfs, Pull-through links and the Ollama registry ask for objects rather than paths, so Hangar checks every file in the Repo's history that holds the object: an object is refused when a file that holds it is refused, when a file that can run code holds it and no Commit with that file is scanned, and when no Commit of the Repo holds it. In a Partial mirror, a pickle that is not in the Arsenal has no scan result, so it is refused until a Pull brings it in and the scan reads it.

The setting applies to every way a file leaves Hangar: huggingface_hub and other Hub API clients, the web UI, git-lfs, git clone and git fetch, Pull-through links, the Ollama registry and zip exports. Hub API and web UI downloads can go ahead with accept_risk=1 in the URL; git-lfs and Ollama answer with a 403 and the reason, and a zip export of a folder with such a file is refused. A git clone or fetch sends every Commit, so it is refused while any Commit holds a file stored in git rather than LFS that would be refused; files in LFS download through git-lfs, which checks each one. The Hub's default .gitattributes, which Hangar applies to new Repos, stores every pickle format in LFS, so this only affects Repos that changed it. Hangar also refuses clones of a Repo whose history is too long to check (more than 20,000 Commits); use huggingface_hub for those.

Links that Hangar signs, for git-lfs, Pull-through and zip export downloads, are checked again when they are used, so a link issued before you turned the setting on, or before the scan finished, stops working. In redirect storage mode, presigned links go straight to the Blob store, so Hangar checks them only when it issues them, and they work until they expire.

docs.title: Choose what to block
docs.text:
The scan classifies each import a pickle makes against lists of known safe and known dangerous functions. Imports on the deny list make a file Unsafe imports; imports on neither list make it Suspicious imports. The deny list cannot be complete, so a function that runs code and is on neither list is reported as suspicious, not unsafe.

What to block scan_block_level Refuses Use it when Unsafe files (default) unsafe Files with imports on the deny list Users download scikit-learn, joblib or full-model pickles, whose model classes from sklearn or transformers are on neither list. Unsafe and suspicious files suspicious Also files with imports on neither list, as torch.load(weights_only=True) does Users should load only weights. Most scikit-learn models and pickles of whole models are refused.

Either way, a user who has reviewed a file can download it through the Hub API or the web UI with accept_risk=1.

docs.title: What the scan cannot catch
docs.text:
• With What to block set to Unsafe files, a function that runs code and is on neither list downloads, reported as suspicious. Review files with suspicious imports before you load them, or load them with torch.load(weights_only=True).
  • Files are checked by name. A pickle with another name, such as one a Repo's trust_remote_code Python loads, is not scanned; trust_remote_code already runs the Repo's Python code, so trust the Repo before you use it.
  • Repos with more than 20,000 Commits, or more than 50,000 LFS files in their history, are checked for objects only in the history Hangar can walk.

docs.title: Verify the image
docs.text:
Images are signed with cosign keyless signing from the release workflow, with an SPDX SBOM attestation and SLSA build provenance. The signing identity is the release workflow at the release tag, refs/tags/v<version>, because a tag push is the only thing that starts a release:

Replace 1.2.3 with the version you run:

cosign verify ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:1.2.3 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/hangar-hub/hangar/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v.+$' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
cosign verify-attestation --type spdxjson ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:1.2.3 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/hangar-hub/hangar/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v.+$' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:1.2.3 --owner hangar-hub

The Helm chart is signed by the same workflow. Verify it the same way:

cosign verify ghcr.io/hangar-hub/charts/hangar:1.2.3 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/hangar-hub/hangar/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v.+$' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

Release archives come with checksums.txt, signed the same way into a Sigstore bundle (checksums.txt.sigstore.json), and an SPDX SBOM per archive (<archive>.spdx.json). Check the signature, then the archive you downloaded against checksums.txt:

cosign verify-blob checksums.txt --bundle checksums.txt.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/hangar-hub/hangar/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v.+$' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c checksums.txt

docs.title: Report a vulnerability
docs.text: See the security policy.

docs.title: Storage backends
docs.text: The Blob store holds LFS objects, git packs and upload staging. Choose the filesystem or any S3-compatible store with storage.backend. Keys are the same on both, so you can move between them with backup and restore.

docs.title: Filesystem
docs.text:
storage:
  backend: fs
  fs:
    path: /var/lib/hangar/blobs

Writes go to a temporary file that is renamed into place, so readers never see partial objects, and nothing relies on file locks. That makes NFS and SMB mounts usable, also from several processes, because the database coordinates everything. Downloads stream through Hangar.

docs.title: S3-compatible stores
docs.text:
storage:
  backend: s3
  s3:
    endpoint: s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com   # host[:port]; prefix http:// for plain HTTP
    region: eu-west-2
    bucket: hangar
    prefix: ""                             # optional key prefix inside the bucket
    access_key_id: ""                      # empty: the default credential chain, IRSA or Workload Identity
    secret_access_key: ""
    use_path_style: false
    download_mode: redirect                # redirect | proxy
    upload_mode: direct                    # direct | proxy
    presign_ttl: 1h
    retries: 5                             # resend a failed part or object upload; 0 = never
    stall_timeout: 2m                      # cancel and retry a request that makes no progress
    startup_wait: 5m                       # keep trying to reach the bucket at start; 0 = exit at once
  • In redirect mode, LFS downloads and zip exports answer with a presigned URL, so file bytes go straight from the store to the client. Clients must reach the store's endpoint; if they cannot, use proxy, which streams through Hangar.
  • In direct upload mode, large-file uploads from git-lfs, huggingface_hub, hangar push and the web UI go straight to presigned URLs, and the UI's Content Security Policy allows the store's origin. Clients must reach the store's endpoint; if they cannot, set upload_mode: proxy, and uploads stream through Hangar into the store. Presigned upload URLs sign no headers, because huggingface_hub sends none, and write to a staging key under tmp/uploads/; Hangar checks the SHA-256 and size of what arrives and copies it into place server-side before anyone can download it.
  • In redirect mode, Ollama model layers redirect to presigned URLs too. Ollama follows a redirect only to a public address unless it pulls with --insecure; see Ollama.
  • At start, a server or worker that cannot reach the bucket keeps trying for startup_wait, logging waiting for the Blob store with the endpoint, the bucket and the error on each attempt, and then exits. While it waits, /healthz answers 200 and /readyz answers 503, so an object store that starts after Hangar, as in some GitOps installs, does not put Hangar into a restart back-off. The filesystem backend is not retried.
Provider Settings Notes AWS S3 endpoint: s3.<region>.amazonaws.com, region, bucket; credentials from the environment, the shared file, the instance profile or IRSA Add a lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads after a few days. MinIO endpoint: minio.example.com:9000 (or http://...), use_path_style: true, region: the region your MinIO is configured with Tested in CI. Use MinIO's own region: us-east-1 only when MinIO has none set, which is its default. If it has one, such as eu-west-2 set with MINIO_SITE_REGION, requests signed for another region fail. mc admin config get <alias> site shows it. Behind nginx, see MinIO behind nginx. MinIO expires stale multipart uploads itself (24 hours by default). Ceph RGW endpoint of the gateway, use_path_style: true Cloudflare R2 endpoint: <account-id>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com, region: auto R2 has no egress charges, which suits redirect mode. Backblaze B2 endpoint: s3.<region>.backblazeb2.com, region: <region> Use an application key limited to the bucket. Garage endpoint of a Garage node, region: garage, use_path_style: true

docs.title: Slow or unreliable links
docs.text:
Hangar often runs on home hardware and uploads to a cloud bucket over a home connection, where a connection can be reset or stall part of the way through a request. Hangar sends each multipart part and each single upload again when the connection fails, makes no progress for stall_timeout, or the store answers with a server error, SlowDown or RequestTimeout. It waits about 1 second before the first retry and doubles the wait each time, up to 30 seconds, for up to retries retries. Errors that describe the request itself, such as AccessDenied or a missing upload, are not retried.

So that a retry can send the same bytes again, Hangar copies each part to a file in the temporary directory (TMPDIR, /tmp in the container image) while it sends it, and deletes the file when the part is done. Each upload in progress uses up to one part of space there: 16 MiB for objects up to 156 GiB, and more for larger objects. Parts read from a file or from memory are rewound instead of copied.

On a congested link, raise stall_timeout rather than retries: after the last bytes leave Hangar they can still wait in the operating system's send buffer and the router's queue, and the store only answers once they arrive.

The automated suite runs against MinIO, and passed against AWS S3 (eu-west-2) on 2026-10-15; the other providers are configured as above but are not part of CI yet. hangar admin doctor checks a write, read and delete, the clock against the store and, in redirect mode, that a presigned URL works from the server.

docs.title: Multipart uploads left behind
docs.text: An upload that a client abandons is aborted when its row expires (lfs.upload_url_ttl). On S3, also add the bucket lifecycle rule AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload (AWS) or rely on the store's own expiry (MinIO), for uploads whose row was lost.

docs.title: Garbage collection and quotas
docs.text:
A scheduled gc Job (gc.schedule, 03:00 daily by default) deletes LFS objects no Repo references once they are older than gc.grace_period (7 days), and git data that is no longer reachable. Admins can see usage by Namespace and set quotas under Admin, Storage.

To collect at once, select Run GC on that page, or run it on the server host with the server configuration:

hangar admin gc            # LFS objects and git data; add --git or --lfs for one of them
hangar admin gc --queue    # queue a gc Job for the running Instance's workers (Postgres)

hangar admin gc reports what it deleted and how much the Blob store holds afterwards. With SQLite, stop the server first.

docs.title: Run the doctor
docs.text:
hangar admin doctor reads the configuration like the server and checks it end to end:

hangar admin doctor --config /etc/hangar/hangar.yaml
docker exec hangar hangar admin doctor     # Postgres setups; with SQLite, stop the server first
Check What it tests configuration Every key is valid. database Hangar can connect. schema Migrations are at the version this binary expects. clock (database) This host's clock is within 30 seconds of Postgres's. blob store A write, read and delete work, and the clock agrees with the store. presigned downloads On S3 in redirect mode, a presigned URL works from this host. git git 2.39 or later is installed. large reads With --large-read, an object of 1100 MiB (or the size you give, such as --large-read=3GiB) is read back whole in one slow request.

It exits with 1 if any check fails, so you can use it in scripts.

--large-read finds a proxy in front of the Blob store that cuts long reads, such as nginx with its default proxy_max_temp_file_size. The doctor writes the object, reads it back at 16 MiB/s, more slowly than the store sends, and deletes it. At the default size this takes over a minute. Run it after putting a proxy in front of MinIO, or when large uploads take many retries to complete. See Large files through nginx.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text:
The server will not start and lists configuration errors. Hangar checks the whole configuration and lists every problem at once. hangar config validate does the same without starting.

"unknown environment variable HANGAR_PORT", or another HANGAR_ name. Hangar reads every environment variable that starts with HANGAR_ as configuration, and refuses to start if one is not a configuration key, so a misspelt key cannot go unnoticed. Only HANGAR_CONFIG and names that start with HANGAR_CLI_ or HANGAR_TEST_ are left alone. The check applies to hangar server, hangar worker, hangar healthcheck, hangar config and the hangar admin commands; client commands such as hangar pull are not affected.

Error: invalid configuration (2 problems):
  - unknown environment variable HANGAR_PORT
  - unknown environment variable HANGAR_ADMIN_PASSWORD

The usual cause is a name meant for another tool. The Docker Compose examples read HANGAR_IMAGE, HANGAR_PORT, HANGAR_PUBLIC_URL, HANGAR_ADMIN_PASSWORD, HANGAR_INSTANCE_KEY and HANGAR_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET from .env and pass the values to Hangar under its own names, and the load tests read HANGAR_URL and HANGAR_TOKEN. If such a name reaches Hangar, for example because you loaded .env into your shell with set -a; . ./.env or passed it to docker run -e, unset it there, or use the configuration key's own variable from the configuration reference, such as HANGAR_SERVER_PUBLIC_URL or HANGAR_SECURITY_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD.

"database is in use by another Hangar process". SQLite allows one process. Stop the other one, or move to Postgres to run several.

Sign-in says "Too many failed sign-in attempts". Someone, perhaps not the user, has sent wrong passwords for the account or from the address. The username's lock does not apply from addresses the user has signed in from with a password in the last 90 days, so they can usually sign in from their usual network. Otherwise wait for the lock to end (at most 15 minutes), or on the server host clear it with hangar admin unlock-sign-in <username> (or --ip <address>, or --all). With SQLite, stop the server first. If every user is throttled at once, check server.trusted_proxies: see TLS and reverse proxies.

Every admin is locked out. On the server host, set a new password with hangar admin reset-password <username>, which prints a generated password once (or reads one with --password-stdin), signs the user out everywhere and clears sign-in throttling. hangar admin create-user <username> --admin creates another Instance admin. With SQLite, stop the server first.

Index or scan results look out of date. hangar admin reindex queues index and scan Jobs for every branch head, or for the Repos you name; the workers run them.

/readyz answers 503. The body lists the failed checks: usually the database, a pending migration (run hangar admin migrate) or the Blob store. A startup failure means the process is still building the Instance; it clears when the process logs hangar started. Each failed check is also logged at warn as readiness check failed, with the check's name and error, so a 503 in the access log can be traced to its cause.

Downloads fail with a 403 from the store, or a TLS error. In S3 redirect mode, clients download straight from the store, so they must reach storage.s3.endpoint and trust its certificate, and the clocks must agree. Use download_mode: proxy if clients cannot reach the store.

Large-file uploads fail with a host lookup or connection error for the store's endpoint. In S3 direct upload mode, git-lfs, huggingface_hub and hangar push upload LFS objects straight to the store, so clients must reach storage.s3.endpoint. Use upload_mode: proxy if they cannot.

huggingface_hub says a Repo does not exist. Private Repos answer as missing without a Token that can read them. Check HF_TOKEN and hangar whoami. For a Mirror, check the Pull finished under Jobs.

load_dataset hangs before it starts. It is waiting for datasets-server.<host>; see Datasets.

Ollama says the server responded with an error over HTTP. Ollama uses HTTPS unless you pass --insecure; see Ollama.

Pulls never start. Check the pull windows (pull.windows) and whether a worker is running: processes in role web do not run Jobs.

git push is rejected. Mirrors are read-only, default branches refuse force-pushes, and non-LFS files over git.max_blob_size are refused. The rejection message says which.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: Set telemetry.log_level: debug for more detail, and telemetry.log_format: text to read logs in a terminal. Every log line inside a request has trace_id and span_id, which match the trace in your tracing backend, and request_id. A server error names its request ID, in the message and the X-Request-Id response header, and the hangar CLI prints it: search the logs for that request_id to find the cause.

docs.title: Still stuck
docs.text: Open a GitHub issue with the output of hangar version and hangar admin doctor, and the log lines around the error, with secrets removed. Get help says which form to use and what to include.

docs.title: Uninstall Hangar
docs.text: Removing Hangar's containers or binary leaves its data where it is. Each section below says how to remove the data too. Where Hangar keeps data lists every location.

docs.title: Keep a copy first
docs.text:
To keep your models and datasets, back up before you remove anything:

  • hangar admin backup writes the database and every LFS object to a folder; see Backup and restore.
  • Or copy the Blob store folder or bucket. Large files are stored whole, under their SHA-256, so you can read them without Hangar.

Keep the Instance key with the backup if you might restore it, but not in the same place.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
docker rm -f hangar
docker volume rm hangar            # the database, the Blob store and secrets.yaml
docker volume rm hangar-backups    # if you made backups into this volume
docker image rm ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:latest   # or the tag you ran

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
From deploy/compose, with the file you started:

docker compose -f quickstart.yaml down       # removes the containers, keeps the volumes
docker compose -f quickstart.yaml down -v    # also deletes the example's volumes, and with them the data

down -v deletes the named volumes the file declares: hangar-data in quickstart.yaml and oidc-keycloak.yaml, and postgres-data and minio-data in postgres-minio.yaml and scale.yaml, which also has its own hangar-data. The .env file holds the passwords and the Instance key; delete it once you no longer need the data.

docs.title: Helm
docs.text:
helm uninstall hangar --namespace hangar

The chart keeps two resources on purpose, so a reinstall over the same data keeps working: the PersistentVolumeClaim (with persistence on) and the Secret with the generated Instance key and admin password. For a release named hangar, delete them with:

kubectl delete pvc hangar --namespace hangar
kubectl delete secret hangar-generated --namespace hangar

Whether deleting the PersistentVolumeClaim also deletes the volume depends on its StorageClass's reclaim policy. If you used Postgres, an S3 bucket or your own Secret (existingSecret), the chart did not create them, so delete them yourself.

docs.title: Binary and Homebrew
docs.text:
Stop the server, then delete the binary, or uninstall the cask:

sudo rm /usr/local/bin/hangar
brew uninstall --cask hangar

Then delete the folders your configuration names: server.data_dir, database.dsn with SQLite, storage.fs.path and git.cache_dir. With the defaults those are /var/lib/hangar and /var/cache/hangar/git; the binary guide puts them under ~/hangar and ~/.cache/hangar/git.

docs.title: The CLI on a workstation
docs.text:
1. Sign out, which removes the saved Token from the OS keychain and the configuration file:

    hangar logout

    The Token stays valid until you revoke it: open Settings, Tokens in the web UI and revoke it, and any other Tokens you no longer use.

  2. Remove the models hangar lmstudio install put into LM Studio. --prune also deletes their files from the Hugging Face cache when no other install uses them:

    hangar lmstudio list
hangar lmstudio remove <repo> --prune

  3. Under Settings, Ollama keys, remove the key you registered. Models you pulled into Ollama stay in Ollama until you remove them with ollama rm.

  4. Delete ~/.config/hangar.

Files that hangar pull downloaded are in the shared Hugging Face cache (~/.cache/huggingface/hub by default), where Python libraries use them too. Remove them from there as you would files downloaded from huggingface.co.

docs.title: Upgrade Hangar
docs.text: Hangar follows semantic versioning. Each release's container image, Helm chart, archives and Homebrew cask carry the same version.

docs.title: Before you upgrade
docs.text:
1. Find the version you run: hangar version, or Admin, System in the web UI.
  2. Read the changelog from your version to the new one. A major version lists what is not backward compatible under BREAKING CHANGES. Notes per version lists anything you need to do.
  3. Back up the database, the Blob store and the Instance key; see Backup and restore. A backup is the only way back to the old version.

hangar admin migrate applies every pending migration, so you can upgrade from any earlier release of the same major version straight to the latest one.

docs.title: Pin a version
docs.text:
latest moves to every new release, so a container restart can upgrade an Instance without anyone choosing to. On an Instance other people rely on, run a version tag instead, and change it when you upgrade:

  • ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:1.2.3 stays on one release.
  • ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:1.2 follows patch releases of 1.2 only.

docs.title: One container
docs.text:
docker pull ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:1.2.3
docker stop hangar && docker rm hangar
docker run -d --name hangar ... ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:1.2.3   # the same options as before

The data is in the volume, so the new container starts with it. A process in role all applies migrations when it starts.

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
Set the new version in .env next to the Compose files, for example HANGAR_IMAGE=ghcr.io/hangar-hub/hangar:1.2.3, then pull it and recreate the containers:

docker compose -f postgres-minio.yaml pull
docker compose -f postgres-minio.yaml up -d

Use the file you started with. In scale.yaml, the one-off migrate service runs hangar admin migrate with the new image, and Compose starts the new web and worker replicas once it has finished.

docs.title: Binary
docs.text:
Download the new archive and replace the binary, as Run the hangar binary shows, then restart the server. With Homebrew:

brew upgrade --cask hangar-hub/tap/hangar

Binaries built with go install report their version as dev, so use a release archive for a server you need to keep track of.

docs.title: Several processes
docs.text:
1. Run the new version's hangar admin migrate once. Migrations only add to the schema within a major version, so processes of the previous version keep working while it runs.
  2. Roll the worker processes, then the web processes. New processes report ready once the schema matches.

docs.title: Helm
docs.text:
The chart version is the Hangar version, so upgrading the chart upgrades Hangar:

helm upgrade hangar oci://ghcr.io/hangar-hub/charts/hangar --version 1.2.3 --namespace hangar -f values.yaml

The chart runs the migration in a pre-upgrade Job, or in an init container in each Pod with migrations.mode: initContainer, and rolls the Deployments for you. With Argo CD, change targetRevision in the Application; see Run with Argo CD.

docs.title: Check the upgrade
docs.text:
• hangar version, or Admin, System, shows the new version.
  • /readyz answers 200. If it answers 503, the body names the check that failed, such as a pending migration.
  • hangar admin doctor checks the configuration, the database, the Blob store and git end to end; see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Notes per version
docs.text: Upgrade What to do 1.4.0, from any earlier 1.x Run hangar admin migrate as usual (migration 0011). A Repo's size is now its total: size_bytes in the native API counts every LFS object the Repo's Commits reference, including the files a Partial mirror has not pulled, and the new present_bytes counts what the Instance holds. Before, size_bytes counted only what the Instance held. The migration fills both for existing Repos, and the size sort and the size_max filter compare the total. The Hub API's usedStorage is still the bytes held. Update hangar on client machines for tab completion; see Turn on tab completion. 1.3.1, from any earlier 1.x Run hangar admin migrate as usual (migrations 0008 to 0010). On an HTTPS Instance, everyone signs in to the web UI once more, because the session cookie is now __Host-hangar_session. UI sessions unused for 7 days now end (security.session_idle_timeout). Device logins give a read Token unless the user chooses write, and their Tokens expire after 30 days. Registering an Ollama key needs a signature from the key: update hangar on machines that run hangar ollama key register. 1.3.0, from any earlier 1.x Run hangar admin migrate as usual (migrations 0004 to 0007). 1.1.x or 1.2.x, from any earlier 1.x Nothing. No release from 1.0.0 to 1.2.3 changed the database schema or the Helm chart's values. 1.2.0 added ui.docs_url, which defaults to https://hangar.page/; on an air-gapped network, point it at your copy of the docs.

docs.title: Downgrades
docs.text: Migrations do not run backwards. To go back to an earlier version, restore a backup made with it.

docs.title: Sign in with OIDC
docs.text: Hangar signs people in through any OpenID Connect provider, with PKCE, alongside or instead of local accounts. You can configure more than one provider.

docs.title: What every provider needs
docs.text:
1. In the provider, create a confidential web application (client) with:
  2. the redirect URI <public_url>/auth/oidc/<id>/callback, where <id> is the provider ID you choose in Hangar, such as https://hangar.example.com/auth/oidc/keycloak/callback;
  3. the openid, profile and email scopes, and a groups claim if you want to map groups.
  4. Add the provider to Hangar's configuration:
oidc:
  providers:
    - id: keycloak                    # in the callback URL; keep it stable
      name: Keycloak                  # on the sign-in button
      issuer: https://sso.example.com/realms/example
      client_id: hangar
      client_secret: ""               # better: set it in a secret, see below
      scopes: [openid, profile, email, groups]
      claims: {username: preferred_username, email: email, name: name, groups: groups}
      admin_groups: [hangar-admins]   # members become Instance admins
      org_mappings:
        - {group: ml-team, org: ml, role: write}
      auto_create_users: true         # create a User on first sign-in

As an environment variable, oidc.providers is a JSON array:

HANGAR_OIDC_PROVIDERS='[{"id":"keycloak","name":"Keycloak","issuer":"https://sso.example.com/realms/example","client_id":"hangar","client_secret":"...","scopes":["openid","profile","email","groups"],"auto_create_users":true}]'

Keep the variable in a secret, because it holds the client secret.

docs.title: Groups, admins and Organisations
docs.text:
• admin_groups: members of these groups become Instance admins on every sign-in, and stop being admins when they leave the group.
  • org_mappings: members of a group become Members of an Organisation with a Role. Hangar creates the Organisation if it does not exist.
  • claims.groups: the claim that lists groups. Some providers need a mapper or extra scope to include it; the provider pages say how.

docs.title: Local accounts alongside OIDC
docs.text:
With OIDC on, you can turn off password sign-in (security.local_login: false). The bootstrap admin can still sign in with a password, as a break-glass account if the provider is down.

People who already have a local account can link a provider under Settings, Profile, Sign-in providers.

docs.title: Names, emails and passwords
docs.text:
Hangar copies the display name and email from the provider's claims only when it creates a User, on the first sign-in, and treats the email as confirmed only when the claims mark it verified (email_verified). After that they belong to the User, who can change them under Settings, Profile; later sign-ins do not overwrite them. A new email a user types waits for the confirmation link an admin sends to it, like anyone's.

A first sign-in whose verified email belongs to an existing User is refused until that User signs in and links the provider. Only a verified email counts: one a user typed and never confirmed blocks nobody. Admin groups and Organisation mappings are the only things Hangar takes from the provider at every sign-in.

A User that OIDC created has no Hangar password, so Settings, Profile tells them to change their password with the provider, and POST /api/hangar/v1/me/password answers 403. A local User who links a provider keeps their Hangar password and can still change it.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text: Keycloak, Authentik, Microsoft Entra ID, Google, Okta, GitLab and UniFi Identity. Any other OpenID Connect provider works the same way.

docs.title: OIDC with Authentik
docs.text:
1. In Authentik, open Applications, Providers, Create, OAuth2/OpenID Provider:
  2. Client type Confidential.
  3. Redirect URI (strict): https://hangar.example.com/auth/oidc/authentik/callback.
  4. Scopes: openid, email, profile. Authentik includes a groups claim in the profile scope.
  5. Create an Application named Hangar with the slug hangar that uses the provider.
  6. Configure Hangar with the client ID and secret:
oidc:
  providers:
    - id: authentik
      name: Authentik
      issuer: https://auth.example.com/application/o/hangar/
      client_id: <client ID>
      scopes: [openid, profile, email]
      claims: {username: preferred_username, email: email, name: name, groups: groups}
      admin_groups: [hangar-admins]
      auto_create_users: true

The issuer is the application's OpenID Configuration Issuer, with the trailing slash.

docs.title: OIDC with Microsoft Entra ID
docs.text:
1. In the Entra admin centre, open App registrations, New registration:
  2. Redirect URI, platform Web: https://hangar.example.com/auth/oidc/entra/callback.
  3. Under Certificates & secrets, create a client secret.
  4. Under Token configuration, Add groups claim, choose Security groups and, for the ID token, Group ID (or sAMAccountName for groups synced from Active Directory).
  5. Configure Hangar:
oidc:
  providers:
    - id: entra
      name: Microsoft
      issuer: https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant ID>/v2.0
      client_id: <application (client) ID>
      scopes: [openid, profile, email]
      claims: {username: preferred_username, email: email, name: name, groups: groups}
      admin_groups: [<object ID of the admins group>]
      org_mappings:
        - {group: <object ID of a group>, org: ml, role: write}
      auto_create_users: true

Entra sends group object IDs, not names, so use the IDs in admin_groups and org_mappings. preferred_username is the user principal name, such as alice@example.com. Hangar usernames cannot contain @, so if sign-in reports an invalid username, map claims.username to a claim without one, such as an optional login_hint or a custom claim with the user's alias.

People in more than 200 groups get no groups claim in the token; give Hangar's application an assignment to the groups that matter, or use app roles.

docs.title: OIDC with GitLab
docs.text:
GitLab.com and self-managed GitLab are OpenID Connect providers.

  1. In GitLab, open Admin, Applications (instance-wide) or a group's Settings, Applications, and add an application:
  2. Redirect URI: https://hangar.example.com/auth/oidc/gitlab/callback.
  3. Confidential: on. Scopes: openid, profile, email.
  4. Configure Hangar:
oidc:
  providers:
    - id: gitlab
      name: GitLab
      issuer: https://gitlab.example.com
      client_id: <application ID>
      scopes: [openid, profile, email]
      claims: {username: nickname, email: email, name: name, groups: groups_direct}
      admin_groups: [platform/hangar-admins]
      auto_create_users: true

GitLab lists a user's groups by full path in the groups_direct claim.

docs.title: OIDC with Google
docs.text:
1. In the Google Cloud console, open APIs & Services, Credentials, Create credentials, OAuth client ID:
  2. Application type Web application.
  3. Authorised redirect URI: https://hangar.example.com/auth/oidc/google/callback.
  4. Configure Hangar:
oidc:
  providers:
    - id: google
      name: Google
      issuer: https://accounts.google.com
      client_id: <client ID>.apps.googleusercontent.com
      scopes: [openid, profile, email]
      claims: {username: email, email: email, name: name}
      auto_create_users: true

Google sends no groups, so grant admin rights and Organisation Membership in Hangar. To limit sign-in to your Google Workspace domain, set the consent screen's user type to Internal.

docs.title: OIDC with Keycloak
docs.text:
Try it locally first with the Keycloak Compose example, which imports a ready realm.

  1. In your realm, open Clients, Create client:
  2. Client type OpenID Connect, client ID hangar.
  3. Client authentication on; Standard flow on; other flows off.
  4. Valid redirect URIs: https://hangar.example.com/auth/oidc/keycloak/callback.
  5. Copy the client secret from the Credentials tab.
  6. Add a groups claim: Client scopes, Create client scope named groups, then Mappers, By configuration, Group Membership, token claim name groups, Full group path off. Add the scope to the hangar client as a default scope.
  7. Configure Hangar:
oidc:
  providers:
    - id: keycloak
      name: Keycloak
      issuer: https://sso.example.com/realms/example
      client_id: hangar
      scopes: [openid, profile, email, groups]
      claims: {username: preferred_username, email: email, name: name, groups: groups}
      admin_groups: [hangar-admins]
      auto_create_users: true

and set the client secret in a secret, such as HANGAR_OIDC_PROVIDERS as JSON.

Hangar and the browser must both reach the issuer URL exactly as configured, because the issuer in tokens has to match it.

docs.title: OIDC with Okta
docs.text:
1. In the Okta admin console, open Applications, Create App Integration, OIDC - OpenID Connect, Web Application:
  2. Sign-in redirect URI: https://hangar.example.com/auth/oidc/okta/callback.
  3. Assign the people or groups who may use Hangar.
  4. To send groups, open the authorisation server's Claims (or the app's Sign On, OpenID Connect ID Token) and add a groups claim with a filter such as Matches regex .*.
  5. Configure Hangar:
oidc:
  providers:
    - id: okta
      name: Okta
      issuer: https://example.okta.com/oauth2/default
      client_id: <client ID>
      scopes: [openid, profile, email, groups]
      claims: {username: preferred_username, email: email, name: name, groups: groups}
      admin_groups: [hangar-admins]
      auto_create_users: true

docs.title: OIDC with UniFi Identity
docs.text:
UniFi Identity Enterprise can act as an OpenID Connect provider for internal applications.

  1. In UniFi Identity Enterprise, add an application with the OIDC sign-on method:
  2. Redirect URI: https://hangar.example.com/auth/oidc/unifi/callback.
  3. Copy the client ID, client secret and issuer URL that it shows.
  4. Assign the users or groups who may use Hangar.
  5. Configure Hangar:
oidc:
  providers:
    - id: unifi
      name: UniFi
      issuer: <issuer URL from the application>
      client_id: <client ID>
      scopes: [openid, profile, email, groups]
      claims: {username: preferred_username, email: email, name: name, groups: groups}
      admin_groups: [hangar-admins]
      auto_create_users: true

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Hangar is one Go binary with an embedded React UI. The full design is in the specification; this is the short version.

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
┌──────────────── load balancer ────────────────┐
               │                                               │
        hangar --role=web (×N)                       hangar --role=worker (×M)
               │   │                                           │   │
               │   └────────────── Postgres ───────────────────┘   │
               │                (metadata, refs, Jobs, sessions)   │
               └────────────────── Blob store ─────────────────────┘
                     (LFS objects, git data, upload staging)
   clients ──────► web replicas; LFS downloads redirect to presigned S3 URLs

web processes are stateless; everything shared lives in the database or the Blob store. Role all runs both in one process, with SQLite. See Scaling.

docs.title: One source of truth: git
docs.text:
Every Repo is a git repository. The Hub HTTP API, git smart HTTP and the web UI are views of the same Commits, and one package (internal/repo) is the only code that writes Commits or refs. Ref updates are compare-and-swap in a database transaction, after the pack bytes are durable in the Blob store, so two concurrent pushes to a branch cannot both win, on any replica.

git packs live in the Blob store and are cached on local disk per replica. Large files are LFS objects stored whole, addressed by SHA-256, and deduplicated across the Instance.

docs.title: Protocols on one host
docs.text: Path Served by /api/hangar/v1/... Native API (OpenAPI) /api/..., /{ns}/{name}/resolve/... Hugging Face Hub API /{ns}/{name}.git/... git smart HTTP and git-lfs /v2/... Ollama registry /xet-cas/... Xet uploads /datasets-server/..., or the datasets-server.<host> name Dataset Viewer API Everything else The web UI, with the same page URLs as huggingface.co

docs.title: Background work
docs.text: Pulls, indexing, scans, garbage collection, Parquet exports and webhook deliveries run as Jobs from a queue in the database, with leases, deduplication and schedules. Pull bandwidth is limited by a token bucket shared through the database, so the cap holds across workers.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text: Package Does internal/repo, internal/gitstore Repos, Commits, refs and git storage internal/hfapi The Hub HTTP API internal/gitserver git smart HTTP and git-lfs internal/upstream Upstreams, Discover, Pulls and Dependencies internal/jobs, internal/gc The Job queue, workers and garbage collection internal/blob The filesystem and S3 Blob stores internal/auth, internal/org, internal/audit Users, sessions, Tokens, OIDC, Organisations and the audit log internal/index, internal/scan Metadata extraction and security scanning internal/datasets Configs, Splits, Parquet export and the Dataset Viewer internal/ollama, internal/xet The Ollama registry and Xet uploads internal/cli The client and admin commands ui/ The web UI

docs.title: Contributing to Hangar
docs.text: Thanks for helping. This page covers setting up, testing and sending changes.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• For anything bigger than a small fix, open an issue first, so we can agree on the approach.
  • Hangar's behaviour is specified in docs/spec/. Compatibility with the Hugging Face Hub is the product: check behaviour against docs/spec/03-hf-api.md and the huggingface_hub source, not memory.
  • Use the vocabulary in CONTEXT.md in code, docs and UI copy.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
You need Go (the version in go.mod), Node.js 24 with corepack, Docker (for Postgres and MinIO in tests), git 2.39 or later with git-lfs, and uv for the Python compatibility suites. The repository has a dev container (.devcontainer/) with all of them.

git clone https://github.com/hangar-hub/hangar.git
cd hangar
make build        # the UI and bin/hangar
make dev          # the server on :8080 and the UI with live reload on :5173

docs.title: make targets
docs.text: Target Does make build Build the UI and the hangar binary into bin/. make dev Run the server with live UI reload. make lint Go, UI and house style linters. make test Unit and integration tests, on SQLite and Postgres and against MinIO (needs Docker). Each package may run for 30 minutes (GO_TEST_TIMEOUT), because git-heavy packages can pass but take longer than go test's 10-minute default on a busy machine. make test-compat The client compatibility suites in compat/. make generate Regenerate the API code, the configuration, CLI and metrics references and the dashboards. CI fails if they are out of date. make lint-deploy Lint the Helm chart, check the Compose files, and check that every GitHub Action the workflows use exists at the version they name, and that every job that runs uv installs it (needs yq). make image Build the container image. make docs Build the documentation site. make demo-serve Build the mock demo that runs at https://demo.hangar.page/ and run it locally under wrangler dev on port 8787. make test-demo runs the Playwright suite against it. make help Everything else.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Tests ship with code. Every change needs tests that fail without it, and make lint test must pass. Database tests run on SQLite and Postgres with dbtest.ForEachDriver; the Blob store conformance suite runs on the filesystem and MinIO. Coverage must stay at 75% per package, 85% for internal/auth, internal/repo, internal/gitserver and internal/hfapi.

Never skip, disable or weaken a test to get a change through. No stubs, placeholder data or TODOs in shipped code; fakes live in *test packages.

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
• Go: gofmt and goimports, checked by golangci-lint.
  • UI: Biome.
  • Prose, UI text, error messages and CLI help: the Google developer documentation style guide, in British English, with no em dashes. make lint-style catches the dashes, common American spellings and a space before a percent sign in the docs (scripts/check-spelling.sh), tests the docs cite by a name or file that does not exist (scripts/check-test-citations.py), and relative Markdown links that name no file (scripts/check-doc-links.py), including in docs/spec and docs/build, which the docs site does not build; put API names and identifiers in backticks and quotations in double quotes so the spelling check leaves them alone.
  • Never log or record on spans: tokens, passwords, cookies, presigned URLs or Authorization headers.

docs.title: Commits and pull requests
docs.text:
• Use Conventional Commits, such as feat(hfapi): support list_repo_likers or fix(cli): resume downloads after a 416. release-please builds the changelog from them.
  • Keep pull requests focused, and fill in the template.
  • Do not add attribution lines to commits or pull requests.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
release-please keeps a release pull request open on main. It proposes the next version from the Conventional Commits merged since the last release and writes the changelog entry. Merging it tags the release, and the release workflow publishes the binaries, the container image, the Helm chart and the documentation.

  • release-please reads the current version from .release-please-manifest.json. initial-version in release-please-config.json set the version of the first release, 1.0.0, and has no effect on later releases.
  • release-please creates the GitHub release with the changelog entry as its notes. GoReleaser then uploads the binaries and appends the install and verification notes from release.footer in .goreleaser.yaml.
  • After changing .goreleaser.yaml or release.yml, run make release-rehearsal. It runs the release's SBOM and cosign steps on this machine with a throwaway key and a local registry, and verifies what they produce. Only the GitHub OIDC identity of keyless signing needs a real release run.
  • To release a version other than the one release-please proposes, add a Release-As: x.y.z footer to a commit on main, for example with git commit --allow-empty -m "chore: release 1.2.0" -m "Release-As: 1.2.0".
